arc.title: Palaces to Provinces
arc.sub: the Bronze Age collapse and the empires built on its ruins, 1363 to 486 BCE
arc.thesis: The Late Bronze Age order rested on a handful of palaces that controlled scarce metal, writing and long-distance trade, and it fell together because each part depended on the others; the iron, alphabet and coin that followed spread the means of war and trade to small states, and the empires that reunited the Near East after 911 BCE held it to the degree that they taxed that wider world through provinces while leaving its local elites a stake.
assumptions: Assumes the collapse was a cascade through linked palaces; a single dominant cause, such as one drought or one wave of invaders, would weaken the first half of the thesis.
Assumes iron and the alphabet lowered the cost of war and administration fast enough to matter politically, though iron took two to three centuries to displace bronze.
Assumes Assyria, Babylon and Persia form one line of development, so that Persian methods can be read as lessons drawn from Assyria's fall.
arc.disconfirm: If the thesis were wrong, the empire that ruled by deportation and direct provinces should have lasted as long as the one that ruled through local kings and gods. Assyria lasted 133 years from Tiglath-Pileser III's reforms to the fall of Nineveh; Persia lasted about 220 from Cyrus to Alexander. The comparison is confounded by the megadrought that weakened Assyria's heartland from about 675 BCE.
arc.awkward: The empire that rebuilt the Near East was the one great power of the Bronze Age club that never fell. Assyria kept its kings, its capital at Assur and its cuneiform scribes through the collapse, and its Iron Age empire still wrote royal annals in Akkadian on clay in 612 BCE.

stories.title: The Linked Palaces
stories.sub: the Late Bronze Age system and its collapse, 1363 to 1075 BCE
stories.thesis: The great kings of Egypt, Hatti, Babylon, Mitanni and Assyria ran an interdependent system of gift exchange, dynastic marriage and metal trade that kept the strongest of them at peace after 1259 BCE, and the same interdependence turned drought, famine and raiding after 1210 BCE into the collapse of the whole.
assumptions: Assumes the palace archives, which record diplomacy and trade, describe how the system worked as well as how its kings wished it to look.
Assumes the destructions between about 1190 and 1130 BCE are connected; they cluster within two generations and rarely within one year.
Assumes Egypt's survival is the same collapse at lower intensity, with a slower decline in place of sudden destruction.
stories.disconfirm: If the thesis were wrong, the destructions should trace to one agent or one event: the Sea Peoples, a single drought or a war of all against all. The evidence points to several at once: tree rings show a three-year drought in Anatolia from about 1198 BCE, the Ugarit letters show raids by sea, and Hattusa was emptied by its own court before it burned.
stories.awkward: Assyria, a full member of the club and Hatti's main rival, lost territory to the Aramaeans and kept its king, its capital and its scribes; whatever broke the system left one of its great powers standing.

chapters.title: The club
chapters.s1: By the 1350s BCE five great kings ran the eastern Mediterranean as a club of equals, trading gold, metal and princesses under rules of reciprocity that each of them tested.
chapters.s2: The Amarna letters, some 380 tablets in Akkadian cuneiform from Pharaoh Akhenaten's capital, show the mechanics: the kings of Egypt, Babylon, Mitanni, Hatti and Alashiya called each other brother and bargained over gifts with the precision of merchants. Membership was contested; the Babylonian King Burna-Buriash II protested that Assyrian envoys at the Egyptian court were his vassals, and Egypt received them anyway, which admitted Assyria's Ashur-uballit I to the club. The Hittite King Suppiluliuma I sacked the Mitanni capital at Washukanni around 1345 BCE, and Mitanni's lands were divided between Hatti and Assyria. The metal flows beneath the diplomacy appear in the Uluburun wreck off southern Turkey: about ten tons of copper and one ton of tin, the ratio for bronze, with 175 glass ingots. Tin came from mines as far away as Central Asia, so every palace depended on routes it could not control.

chapters.title: Kadesh and the treaty
chapters.s1: Egypt and Hatti fought to a draw at Kadesh in 1274 BCE and then signed the oldest surviving peace treaty, which held for the rest of the Bronze Age.
chapters.s2: Pharaoh Ramesses II carved Kadesh as a victory on five temples; the Hittites kept Kadesh and Amurru. In 1259 BCE Ramesses and the Hittite King Hattusili III agreed to non-aggression, mutual defence and the return of fugitives, a clause with a live target in Hattusili's deposed nephew Urhi-Teshub, who had fled to Egypt. The original silver tablets are lost; the text survives in hieroglyphs at Karnak and the Ramesseum and in Akkadian on clay from Hattusa. Ramesses married Hattusili's daughter around 1245 BCE. Peace in Syria freed Assyria in the east: King Tukulti-Ninurta I beat the Hittites at Nihriya and around 1225 BCE took Babylon and carried off the statue of Marduk, so the club entered its last decades with one rising power and two tired ones.

chapters.title: Strain
chapters.s1: From the 1210s BCE the system came under strain at several points at once: famine in Hatti, invasion of Egypt from the west and drought on the Anatolian plateau.
chapters.s2: Pharaoh Merneptah recorded that he shipped grain 'to keep alive this land of Hatti', and the Hittite Queen Puduhepa had already written to Ramesses II that she had no grain in her lands. In his fifth year, about 1208 BCE, Merneptah beat a Libyan invasion of the western Delta that brought Sherden, Shekelesh, Lukka and other seaborne allies; his inscriptions count 6,000 enemy dead and 9,000 prisoners. The stele that records the campaign also holds the first mention of Israel. Juniper rings from central Anatolia record a severe drought from about 1198 to 1196 BCE, three dry years on a plateau whose court lived from storehouses. Each shock alone had precedents and had been survived; the danger lay in their coinciding while the palaces had committed their reserves and fleets to one another.

chapters.title: Cascade
chapters.s1: Between about 1190 and 1175 BCE the palaces of Ugarit, Hatti and Mycenaean Greece fell within a generation, and Egypt held its frontier only by fighting in the Delta.
chapters.s2: Ugarit's last king, Ammurapi, wrote to the king of Alashiya that enemy ships had burned his towns while his own troops and fleet were away in Hittite service; a letter from Chancellor Bay of Egypt, in office about 1194 to 1192 BCE, places the city's destruction after that date. The Hittite court left Hattusa before it burned, and the Hittite state ended with King Suppiluliuma II. The fire that destroyed the Palace of Nestor at Pylos around 1180 BCE baked its Linear B archive, which records rowers and detachments assigned to watch the coast. Around 1175 BCE Pharaoh Ramesses III fought the Peleset, Tjeker and Sherden in the Nile Delta and carved the victory at Medinet Habu. The Sea Peoples were one cause among several: displaced people as much as raiders, they struck palaces that had already lost the grain and metal flows that made them defensible.

chapters.title: Egypt shrinks
chapters.s1: Egypt came through the collapse with its state intact and spent the next century losing its empire, its revenue and its unity.
chapters.s2: Around 1157 BCE the royal tomb-builders of Deir el-Medina stopped work after going eighteen days without grain rations, the first recorded strike. Two years later a harem plot killed Ramesses III; a CT scan of his mummy in 2012 showed his throat had been cut to the bone. The Egyptian garrisons in Canaan fell one by one, Megiddo and Lachish by about 1130 BCE and the fortress at Jaffa around 1125 BCE. With the death of Ramesses XI in 1077 BCE the kingdom split between a pharaoh at Tanis and the high priests of Amun at Thebes. The Story of Wenamun records the new standing: an envoy sent for cedar was made to pay in silver at Byblos, and the prince of Byblos produced his fathers' accounts to show that earlier pharaohs had paid too.

stories.today: The collapse is a standard case in the study of systemic risk: linked states falling together after a cluster of shocks. The Uluburun cargo is on display at the Bodrum Museum of Underwater Archaeology in Turkey, and the Hittite copy of the 1259 BCE treaty is in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums.

stories.title: The Small-State Interval
stories.sub: Neo-Hittites, Aramaeans, Phoenicians and Greeks, 1180 to 832 BCE
stories.thesis: For three centuries after the collapse no power could tax the Levant and Anatolia, and small states (Neo-Hittite, Aramaean, Phoenician, Philistine, Israelite and Greek) filled the space with cheaper tools of war, writing and trade, though they never combined for long against a returning empire.
assumptions: Assumes the absence of a hegemon is the main fact of the period and that the small states filled a vacuum.
Assumes the alphabet's political effect came through cheaper administration and trade, which is better evidenced for Phoenician merchants than for kings.
Assumes the Greek case belongs with the Levantine one, though the Aegean lost writing entirely for some four centuries.
stories.disconfirm: If the thesis were wrong, a single power should have taxed the region before Assyria returned, or the small states should have combined into a lasting federation when it did. Qarqar is the test: eleven kings combined against Assyria in 853 BCE, and within twelve years the coalition had broken apart and its members were paying tribute.
stories.awkward: Iron arrived late. Bloomery smelting in the southern Levant is dated to about 930 BCE and bronze stayed in common use for weapons into the ninth century, so most of the small states formed before the cheap metal that is supposed to explain them.

chapters.title: The heirs
chapters.s1: Where the Hittite empire had been, its provincial branches and their neighbours carried on as small kingdoms, and no power could tax the region for three centuries.
chapters.s2: Kuzi-Teshub, son of the last Hittite viceroy at Carchemish, took the title Great King around 1180 BCE, and his line ruled Carchemish and Melid, carving inscriptions in Luwian hieroglyphs that continue the imperial tradition. On the southern coast of Canaan, locally made Aegean-style pottery and Aegean burial customs mark the settlement of the Philistines at Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, Gath and Gaza; ancient DNA from Ashkelon shows a southern European component that was diluted within two centuries. Assyria tried to hold the Euphrates: King Tiglath-Pileser I campaigned repeatedly against Aramaean tribes and reached the Mediterranean at Arvad, and by his death in 1076 BCE the Aramaeans were pressing on the Assyrian heartland. Aramaean chiefs took over most of the Syrian kingdoms over the next two centuries, which is why Assyrian records name them 'Bit-', the house of a founding ancestor, as in Bit-Adini and Bit-Agusi.

chapters.title: The alphabet
chapters.s1: In the ports that escaped destruction, a script of 22 consonant signs made writing cheap enough for merchants, and the Phoenician cities became the commercial hub of a Mediterranean with no great power.
chapters.s2: Byblos, Sidon and Tyre came through the collapse with their harbours working. The Phoenician alphabet, standard by about 1050 BCE, could be learned by a merchant's clerk where cuneiform needed years of scribal school, and it passed to the Aramaeans, the Israelites and later the Greeks. King Hiram I of Tyre, who ruled about 980 to 947 BCE, joined the city's two islands, built a temple to Melqart and sent cedar and craftsmen to Jerusalem in exchange for wheat and oil. Tyre's traders settled Cyprus, founded Carthage around 814 BCE and reached the Atlantic. Iron became the common metal of the Levant in the same centuries; its ores were found almost everywhere, where bronze had depended on tin carried along a few long routes.

chapters.title: The Aegean
chapters.s1: Greece fell further than the Levant, losing its palaces, its writing and much of its population, and its recovery began when eastern trade returned.
chapters.s2: After the palaces burned, Linear B went out of use and Greece was without writing for some four centuries. Many Peloponnesian settlements were abandoned; from the mid-11th century BCE Greeks from Attica and Euboea crossed the Aegean to settle Samos, Chios and the Ionian coast. At Lefkandi on Euboea, around 950 BCE, a man's ashes were buried in a Cypriot bronze amphora beside a woman wearing gold and a Babylonian pendant already about a thousand years old, with four sacrificed horses, under a building nearly 50 metres long. The Euboeans who traded east brought the alphabet home by about 800 BCE, turning Phoenician letters for consonants Greek lacked into vowels, and led the first Greek colonies to the west.

chapters.title: The coalition
chapters.s1: When Assyria returned to the west, the small states could combine against it for a battle and could not hold together for a decade.
chapters.s2: In 853 BCE eleven kings, led by Hadadezer of Damascus, Irhuleni of Hamath and King Ahab of Israel, met the Assyrian King Shalmaneser III at Qarqar on the Orontes; his monolith credits Ahab with 2,000 chariots and lists 1,000 camels under Gindibu the Arab, the first appearance of Arabs in any record. The battle halted Assyria, and Shalmaneser fought the same coalition several more times over the following decade. By 841 BCE it had broken: Hazael had taken the throne of Damascus and was fighting Israel and Judah, and King Jehu of Israel knelt to Shalmaneser on the Black Obelisk. In the north, Sarduri I made Tushpa on Lake Van the capital of a united Urartu, the one rival in the region built on Assyria's scale. The small states had grown in the absence of a great power and had no institutions for its return.

stories.today: The Phoenician alphabet is the ancestor of the Greek, Latin, Cyrillic, Hebrew and Arabic scripts, used by most of the world's population. The ruins of Carchemish lie at Karkamış on the Turkish-Syrian border, facing the Syrian town of Jarablus.

stories.title: The Assyrian Machine
stories.sub: Neo-Assyria's rise and fall, 911 to 605 BCE
stories.thesis: Assyria built the first empire of provinces, with a standing army, royal governors and mass deportation, and the same machinery that let it conquer from Egypt to Elam bound every loyalty to the king, so that the succession crises of 652 and after 631 BCE let its former subjects destroy it within two decades.
assumptions: Assumes the reforms of Tiglath-Pileser III were a break, where they may only have codified practices built up over the previous century.
Assumes Assyrian royal inscriptions, which inflate victories and omit defeats, can be read for deportation numbers and campaigns at least to an order of magnitude.
Assumes the provinces were the empire's core, though much of its wealth came from vassal tribute that needed no governor.
stories.disconfirm: If the thesis were wrong, Assyria's fall should be explained by outside forces alone: the Median-Babylonian alliance, the Scythians, or the megadrought of about 675 to 550 BCE. The empire had survived the great revolt of 826 to 820 BCE and recovered; the difference after 631 BCE is that its enemies were former subjects organised on its own model.
stories.awkward: Assyria kept winning after the crisis the thesis blames. Ashurbanipal destroyed Susa in 647 BCE, the year after he won the civil war, and the empire held its provinces for another fifteen years before the collapse began.

chapters.title: Reconquest
chapters.s1: Assyria, the one Bronze Age great power that never fell, rebuilt its army from 911 BCE and spent a century retaking lands it regarded as its own.
chapters.s2: King Adad-nirari II and his successors campaigned every year to recover the Middle Assyrian provinces from Aramaean rule, treating war as a royal duty owed to the god Ashur. Ashurnasirpal II moved the capital to Kalhu (Nimrud) in 879 BCE and recorded feeding 69,574 guests at its inauguration. Shalmaneser III pushed to the Mediterranean and Lake Van, though the western coalition held him at Qarqar. The model had a flaw: provinces were large and held by magnates, and when Shalmaneser's son Ashur-danin-pal revolted in 826 BCE, the king's own inscriptions say 27 cities including Nineveh went with him. The revolt lasted until 820 BCE, and for much of the next seventy years governors such as the field marshal Shamshi-ilu ran their regions as near-independent lords.

chapters.title: The machine
chapters.s1: King Tiglath-Pileser III answered the magnates by remaking Assyria as a machine of small provinces, royal governors, a standing army and mass deportation, and roughly doubled its territory in eighteen years.
chapters.s2: He took the throne in 745 BCE after a revolt at Kalhu, split the great provinces into smaller ones under royal appointees, erased Shamshi-ilu's name from the records and built a standing core, the kiṣir šarri, alongside the levies. He beat Urartu's Sarduri II near Arpad in 743 BCE, annexed Damascus in 732 BCE and in 729 BCE became the first Assyrian king the Babylonians accepted as their own. Deportation became policy: tens and possibly hundreds of thousands of people were moved to break local loyalties and put labour where the state needed it. Samaria fell in 722 BCE and Sargon II claimed to have deported 27,280 of its people, ending the kingdom of Israel. The deportees carried Aramaic, and Aramaic, written in the alphabet on leather and papyrus, became the empire's second language of government beside Akkadian on clay.

chapters.title: The apex
chapters.s1: Assyria reached its greatest extent when Esarhaddon took Memphis in 671 BCE, at a distance its army could reach and its governors could not hold.
chapters.s2: Sargon II broke Urartu in 714 BCE, sacking the temple of Haldi at Musasir, and was killed in Tabal in 705 BCE; his body was never recovered, which his court read as divine judgment. His son Sennacherib moved the capital to Nineveh, crushed the Levantine revolt of 701 BCE by destroying Lachish and shutting King Hezekiah inside Jerusalem, and in 689 BCE razed Babylon and flooded its site after the Elamites had seized his heir. The Kushite pharaohs who had ruled Egypt since about 727 BCE backed every revolt in the Levant, and Esarhaddon set out to remove them: his first invasion was beaten near Ashkelon in 673 BCE, and the second took Memphis in 671 BCE with Pharaoh Taharqa's wife and son. Egypt revolted as soon as the army left, and Esarhaddon died at Harran in 669 BCE on his way back.

chapters.title: Overreach
chapters.s1: Esarhaddon's division of the succession between two sons produced a civil war in 652 BCE that Assyria won at a cost it never recovered.
chapters.s2: Ashurbanipal received Assyria and his elder brother Shamash-shum-ukin received Babylon under succession oaths sworn by the vassals in 672 BCE. Ashurbanipal's army sacked Thebes in 663 BCE and carried off two obelisks plated in electrum; within seven years Psamtik I of Sais, using Carian and Ionian mercenaries sent by King Gyges of Lydia, had reunited Egypt outside Assyrian control. In 652 BCE Shamash-shum-ukin rebelled with Chaldeans, Aramaeans and Elam, and Babylon fell only in 648 BCE after a two-year siege. Ashurbanipal destroyed Susa in 647 BCE, claimed to have sown salt on Elam and carried off its kings' bones, and so removed the buffer between Mesopotamia and the peoples of the Iranian plateau. His library at Nineveh, perhaps 100,000 texts copied from temples across the empire, survived because the city's fall buried it; when he died around 631 BCE his heirs fought each other for the throne.

chapters.title: The fall
chapters.s1: Former subjects organised on Assyria's own model destroyed it in fourteen years, from Nabopolassar's coronation at Babylon in 626 BCE to the sack of Nineveh in 612 BCE.
chapters.s2: Nabopolassar, a Babylonian leader of obscure origin, was crowned king of Babylon in November 626 BCE while Assyrian claimants fought over the throne. Cyaxares of the Medes ended a Scythian overlordship around 625 BCE and replaced tribal levies with a standing army on Assyrian and Urartian lines. The Medes sacked Assur, the religious capital, in 614 BCE; Cyaxares and Nabopolassar met in its ruins to seal an alliance with a marriage, and their armies took Nineveh after a siege in the summer of 612 BCE. Ashur-uballit II held Harran with Egyptian help until 609 BCE, and the crown prince Nebuchadnezzar destroyed the last Egyptian and Assyrian force at Carchemish in 605 BCE. The Assyrian capitals were left in ruins, and Babylon took over the provinces almost whole.

stories.today: Islamic State fighters bulldozed and blew up much of Nimrud and damaged the gates of Nineveh in 2015 and 2016; restoration began after Iraqi forces retook the Mosul area. The Library of Ashurbanipal's tablets are in the British Museum, where they remain the main source for the Epic of Gilgamesh.

stories.title: The Persian Synthesis
stories.sub: Babylon, Lydia, Media and the Achaemenid empire, 605 to 486 BCE
stories.thesis: Persia absorbed all four heirs of Assyria within 25 years because Cyrus and Darius kept Assyria's provinces, roads and tribute while leaving local officials, gods and languages in place, which made surrender cheaper than resistance for the elites of Media, Lydia, Babylon and Egypt.
assumptions: Assumes the Cyrus Cylinder and the Persian royal inscriptions describe policy, though they are propaganda in a Mesopotamian genre that Assyrian kings also used.
Assumes the Median kingdom was a state Cyrus could inherit; the evidence for a Median empire is mostly Greek and much of it late.
Assumes Darius's reforms completed Cyrus's design, though Darius took power in a coup and had reason to present himself as a restorer.
stories.disconfirm: If the thesis were wrong, the conquests should have been won by force and held by force. The revolts of 522 to 521 BCE are the test: by Darius's own count he fought nineteen battles in a year against nine rival kings, which suggests that the restraint of Cyrus and Cambyses had bought the empire time and little loyalty.
stories.awkward: Babylon opened its gates in 539 BCE after a battle at Opis in which, by the Babylonian chronicle, Cyrus's army killed the people; the cylinder that presents a peaceful liberation leaves the battle out.

chapters.title: Four heirs
chapters.s1: Assyria's fall left four successor kingdoms (Babylon, Media, Lydia and Egypt) in a balance that a treaty of 585 BCE fixed in Anatolia and that lasted a generation.
chapters.s2: Lydia and Media had fought for five years when an eclipse, dated by modern calculation to 28 May 585 BCE, halted a battle; King Alyattes of Lydia and King Cyaxares of Media made the Halys river their border and married Alyattes's daughter Aryenis to Cyaxares's son Astyages. Media had taken the Urartian capital around 590 BCE. Nebuchadnezzar II spent Levantine tribute on Babylon, whose Ishtar Gate of glazed blue brick, built around 569 BCE, was excavated by a German team and partly rebuilt in Berlin. Lydia had begun striking electrum coins in the late seventh century BCE, giving traders metal of guaranteed weight. The balance depended on its kings: Nabonidus, who took Babylon's throne in 556 BCE, spent about ten years at the oasis of Tayma in Arabia while his son Belshazzar governed and Babylon's New Year festival lapsed.

chapters.title: Cyrus
chapters.s1: Cyrus II, the Persian vassal king of Anshan, overturned the balance within a decade by winning over the Median army and then using Media's resources to take Lydia.
chapters.s2: Cyrus's war with his Median overlord Astyages began around 553 BCE and ended in 550 BCE when the Median commander Harpagus and part of the army changed sides and Ecbatana fell. Cyrus spared Astyages and kept Median nobles in high command, so the Median state passed to him with its officers. King Croesus of Lydia crossed the Halys, fought a drawn battle at Pteria and went home for the winter; Cyrus followed, beat him outside Sardis, using camels to frighten the Lydian horses, and took the citadel after fourteen days in 547 or 546 BCE. Harpagus then reduced the Greek cities of Ionia, Caria and Lycia by about 542 BCE, and Persia's frontier with the Greek world dates from his campaigns.

chapters.title: Babylon
chapters.s1: Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BCE with one battle and an appeal to the city's priests, and he governed it as its legitimate king.
chapters.s2: Nabonidus's army met the Persians at Opis on the Tigris and was routed; Sippar opened its gates on 10 October, and Cyrus's commander Ugbaru entered Babylon two days later without a fight. The clay cylinder laid in the foundations of Marduk's temple blames Nabonidus for impiety, names Marduk as the god who chose Cyrus and records the return of gods and people to their cities, in the standard form of a Babylonian building inscription. The temples and the bureaucracy kept working, and contracts in the business archive of the Egibi family of Babylon run on through the conquest, now dated by Cyrus's years. Cyrus was killed beyond the Syr Darya fighting the Massagetae in 530 BCE, and his son Cambyses II took Egypt at Pelusium in 525 BCE, completing Persia's absorption of all four heirs.

chapters.title: Darius
chapters.s1: The death of Cambyses in 522 BCE set off revolts across the empire, and Darius I won the throne by force and then rebuilt the state so that it could outlast another disputed succession.
chapters.s2: Darius and six Persian nobles killed the king they called the impostor Gaumata in September 522 BCE; the Behistun inscription, carved in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian on a cliff above the road to Ecbatana, counts nineteen battles in a year against nine rival kings. He then set the empire in about twenty satrapies paying fixed tribute, improved the roads with relay stations and issued the gold daric. The Persepolis Fortification tablets, over 15,000 Elamite records from 509 to 493 BCE, show the system at work: rations of grain, wine and beer issued to named workers, women as numerous as men among them, and sealed travel passes for officials on the road. Darius took the Indus valley, crossed into Europe against the Scythians in 513 BCE and opened a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea around 497 BCE. The weak point was the western edge: the Ionian cities revolted in 499 BCE with ships from Athens and Eretria, and Darius's answer began the wars with Greece.

stories.today: Iran's last shah made the Cyrus Cylinder the emblem of the 1971 celebration of 2,500 years of monarchy and called it the first charter of human rights, a reading historians reject; when the British Museum lent it to Tehran in 2010 it drew large crowds under the Islamic Republic. A replica is displayed at United Nations headquarters in New York.

arc.title: The Freedom of the Greeks
arc.sub: city-states, hegemony and the outside powers, c. 770 to 146 BCE
arc.thesis: The polis could defend its own autonomy but could not combine it with scale: every Greek bid to lead the others, Athenian, Spartan and Theban, broke within two generations on its allies' demand for autonomy, and the cities passed under outside powers, Persian money, the Macedonian army and finally Rome, each of which proclaimed 'the freedom of the Greeks'.
assumptions: Assumes autonomia was a working political value that moved allies to revolt, and more than a slogan the strong used against their rivals.
Assumes the Athenian empire failed as a hegemony; a case can be made that it was a viable state that lost a war to Persian money and one strategic error in Sicily.
Assumes Macedon and Rome were outside powers; the Macedonian kings claimed Greek descent and competed at Olympia.
arc.disconfirm: If the thesis were wrong, a league built on guarantees of autonomy should have held without an outside paymaster. Two tests: the Second Athenian League of 378, whose charter banned tribute and garrisons and which broke apart in the Social War of 357-355; and the Achaean League, which held most of the Peloponnese together for more than a century and fell only to Rome.
arc.awkward: The Achaean League combined autonomy and scale for 135 years, with a federal citizenship, a common coinage and a general elected each year, and it was Rome that dissolved it. The Greek failure to federate was a failure of the classical powers, Athens, Sparta and Thebes, more than of the polis as a form.

stories.title: The Hoplite Bargain
stories.sub: colonies, tyrants and constitutions, c. 770 to 508 BCE
stories.thesis: The polis took its lasting forms from a bargain between the landowning families and the farmers who stood in their battle line: colonies exported the surplus, tyrants broke the families where the bargain failed, and the durable constitutions, Sparta's by conquest and Athens' by law, gave the hoplite class a share of power.
assumptions: Assumes the hoplite phalanx was in place by the mid-7th century; the date of the 'hoplite revolution' is contested and some put a fully closed phalanx after 500.
Assumes land shortage drove colonisation; trade, exile and civil strife drove many foundations.
Assumes the later Athenian and Spartan traditions about Lycurgus, Solon and Cleisthenes preserve the substance of reforms written down generations afterwards.
stories.disconfirm: If the thesis were wrong, tyrannies should not cluster in the century when the hoplite class was rising, and the constitutions that lasted should have kept that class out of power. Solon's Athens is the closest test: the third property class, the zeugitai who supplied the hoplites, was admitted to the chief magistracy only in 457.
stories.awkward: Athens' founding reforms needed Spartan arms: Spartan King Cleomenes I expelled the tyrant Hippias in 510, and Cleisthenes' reform of 508 survived only because the citizens besieged a second Spartan force on the Acropolis. The democratic polis was founded with outside help and against outside intervention in the same three years.

chapters.title: The colonies
chapters.s1: Between about 770 and 550 BCE the Greek cities sent their surplus sons across the Mediterranean and the Black Sea, and colonisation relieved the land pressure that would otherwise have broken them sooner.
chapters.s2: Euboeans set up the first western post at Pithekoussai on Ischia around 770 to trade for Etruscan iron; Corinth founded Syracuse in 734, Megara founded Byzantium about 667, and Thera sent settlers to Cyrene in 631. Thera's assembly conscripted one son from each household for the Cyrene venture and made refusal to sail a capital offence, which is emigration by order of a city that could not feed its people. Each foundation became a full polis with its own laws, linked to its mother city by cult and sentiment and owing it no tribute. The result was a Greek world several hundred cities wide in which no single state grew stronger. The colonies also carried the alphabet west: a cup found in a grave at Pithekoussai, dated about 730, bears one of the oldest Greek verse inscriptions, and the Latin alphabet descends from the Euboean letters the Etruscans learned there.

chapters.title: Sparta's answer
chapters.s1: Sparta solved its land problem by conquering the plain of Messenia and enserfing its people as helots, and paid for the solution by turning its citizens into a permanent army of occupation.
chapters.s2: Sparta took Messenia in a war of the late 8th century and reconquered it after a revolt usually dated about 660-650, fought by Spartan hoplites to marching songs, the earliest surviving Greek verse that urges men to hold their place in line shield to shield. After the revolt every Spartiate lived on a plot worked by helots and spent his life from the age of seven in state training and the mess, and the citizen body, about 8,000 in 480, was closed to newcomers. Each year the Spartan ephors formally declared war on the helots so that killing one carried no religious pollution. Expansion stopped at Tegea in the 6th century, and around 550 Sparta turned to bilateral alliances in which each member swore to have the same friends and enemies as Sparta: the Peloponnesian League. The arrangement made Sparta the strongest land power in Greece and left it permanently afraid of a helot rising, which limited how long its army could stay away from home.

chapters.title: The tyrants
chapters.s1: Elsewhere the old aristocracies kept the land and the new hoplite farmers wanted a share, and ambitious nobles took power with popular backing; tyranny became the archaic polis's commonest route out of narrow oligarchy.
chapters.s2: Cypselus overthrew the Bacchiad clan at Corinth in 657 and his family ruled about seventy years; the Orthagorids at Sicyon lasted about a century, the longest tyranny the Greeks recorded. At Athens the noble Cylon tried in 632 with troops lent by his father-in-law, the tyrant Theagenes of Megara, and failed. His followers were killed after being promised their lives, and the curse on the Alcmaeonid family held responsible was still being invoked by Sparta in 432 against Pericles, an Alcmaeonid on his mother's side. The Athenian aristocracy's answer was Draco's written code of about 621, which replaced judgment by nobles with published law and made most offences capital. Tyrannies rarely outlived a second generation, and each fall left a citizen body that had learned it could do without the old families.

chapters.title: Solon's settlement
chapters.s1: Solon's reforms of 594 ended debt bondage at Athens and made wealth the test for office in place of birth, which bought the city a generation without civil war and failed to stop a tyrant.
chapters.s2: Solon, elected archon with powers to arbitrate, cancelled debts secured on land and persons, banned loans on the security of the body and brought home Athenians sold abroad for debt. He divided citizens into four classes by the annual yield of their land, the highest at 500 measures, and opened office by class; the thetes, the poorest, received a place in the assembly and the right of appeal to a popular court. His own poems describe him standing with a shield held over both sides, and both sides were dissatisfied. Twice within a decade Athens failed to elect a chief magistrate, and in 561 Peisistratus seized the Acropolis with a bodyguard voted by the assembly. Peisistratus held power three times until his death in 527, funded partly by silver from the Pangaion region of Thrace, and his rule taught Attica's villages to look to Athens.

chapters.title: Cleisthenes
chapters.s1: The tyranny's fall in 510 reopened the aristocratic feud, and Cleisthenes won it in 508 by giving power to the demes and to ten new tribes, which produced the citizen army that fought at Marathon eighteen years later.
chapters.s2: Spartan King Cleomenes I expelled the tyrant Hippias in 510, four years after Hipparchus, his brother, was murdered by Harmodius and Aristogeiton. When his rival Isagoras won the archonship with Spartan backing, Cleisthenes the Alcmaeonid took the people into his faction. His reform replaced the four kinship tribes with ten artificial ones, each built from three blocs drawn from the coast, the inland and the city, so that every tribal regiment mixed men from across Attica; about 139 villages, the demes, became the units of citizenship, and a Council of 500 took fifty men from each tribe. Cleomenes invaded to reverse it and was besieged on the Acropolis by the citizens until he left. In 506 the new army defeated the Boeotians and the Chalcidians of Euboea on a single day, and Athens settled 4,000 of its citizens on Chalcidian land.

stories.today: Marseille, Syracuse, Naples and Istanbul are Greek foundations still occupied as cities. Selection by lot, the Athenian method for filling the Council of 500, is used for modern citizens' assemblies: Ireland's assembly of 2016-2018 drew 99 citizens by lot, and its recommendation led to the 2018 referendum that legalised abortion.

stories.title: Alliance into Empire
stories.sub: from the Ionian Revolt to the Thirty Years' Peace, 499 to 446 BCE
stories.thesis: Persia was beaten at sea by a fleet only Athens could man, and the alliance formed to keep Persia out became an Athenian empire within a generation because most allies paid money instead of ships and Athens spent the money on its own citizens.
assumptions: Assumes Persia's invasions aimed at the conquest of Greece; Persian sources do not mention the wars, and a punitive raid on Athens and Eretria is a possible reading of 490.
Assumes the allies' choice to pay money instead of ships was voluntary at first; some members were compelled from the start.
Assumes tribute paid for Athenian democracy; Athens also had large domestic revenues from Laurion silver and harbour dues.
stories.disconfirm: If the thesis were wrong, the league should have remained an alliance of navies. The test is the count of members still supplying ships: by about 440 only Samos, Chios and Lesbos did, and Samos lost its fleet after its revolt of 440-439.
stories.awkward: The decisive land battle was Spartan: at Plataea in 479 the Spartan hoplites under the regent Pausanias broke the Persian army and killed its commander Mardonius, and the claim that the Athenian fleet saved Greece was an argument Athens made to justify its empire.

chapters.title: The Ionian Revolt
chapters.s1: The Ionian Greek cities under Persian rule revolted in 499 with Athenian help, and Darius I took Athens' part in burning Sardis as reason to bring mainland Greece within his empire's reach.
chapters.s2: Aristagoras, the tyrant of Miletus, turned a failed Persian attack on Naxos into a revolt of the Ionian cities to save his own position. Athens sent twenty ships and Eretria five, and the force burned Sardis, the seat of the Persian governor of Lydia. The revolt spread to the Hellespont and Cyprus before a mainly Phoenician fleet of about 600 ships destroyed the Ionian fleet of 353 at Lade in 494; Miletus was sacked and its people deported to the Persian Gulf. Darius' son-in-law Mardonius then deposed the Ionian tyrants and allowed the cities democracies, a Persian king installing the constitution Athens would claim as its own. Persia's ambition in the Aegean predated the revolt; the revolt gave it a target.

chapters.title: Marathon
chapters.s1: Athens' new citizen army beat a Persian seaborne force at Marathon in 490, which showed that hoplites could beat Persian infantry and made the democracy a state worth punishing a second time.
chapters.s2: Darius sent an expedition under Datis and Artaphernes that razed Eretria and landed at Marathon on the advice of the exiled Athenian tyrant Hippias. About 10,000 Athenians and Plataeans under the polemarch Callimachus and the general Miltiades charged across the plain; Persian dead were counted at 6,400 against 192 Athenians. The Spartans, held at home by a religious law until the full moon, arrived the day after. The 192 were buried on the field under a mound that still stands, an honour no other Athenian war dead received. Persia answered with a far larger invasion, and Xerxes began preparing it after his accession in 486.

chapters.title: Salamis
chapters.s1: The second invasion was decided at sea by a fleet Athens built from a silver strike at Laurion in 483, and Sparta's army finished it at Plataea in 479.
chapters.s2: Themistocles persuaded the assembly to spend the new silver on triremes instead of sharing it among citizens, citing the war with Aegina; Athens had about 200 ships by 480. Xerxes crossed the Hellespont in 480, and at Thermopylae Spartan King Leonidas and about 7,000 allies held the pass for three days while the fleet fought off Artemisium. Athens was evacuated and burned; in September the Greek fleet of about 370 triremes, nearly half of them Athenian, beat the Persian fleet in the straits of Salamis and Xerxes withdrew to Asia. His general Mardonius stayed and was killed at Plataea the next summer by a Spartan-led army. The Athenian fleet was rowed by the thetes, the poorest citizens, and later Athenians traced the radical democracy to the naval crowd that won at Salamis.

chapters.title: The league
chapters.s1: Leadership of the war against Persia passed from Sparta to Athens in 478, and the Delian League's design, ships or money from each member, contained the empire from the start.
chapters.s2: The Spartan regent Pausanias behaved like a Persian satrap at Byzantium, and the Ionian allies asked Athens to lead; Sparta withdrew, relieved to keep its army at home. Aristides assessed the first contributions at 460 talents a year, with the treasury on the sacred island of Delos. Cimon's victory at the Eurymedon around 466 destroyed a Persian fleet and army and removed the immediate threat at the moment Athens began forcing members to stay in: Naxos around 471 and Thasos in 465-463, which lost its walls, fleet and mines. Sparta secretly promised Thasos an invasion of Attica and was stopped only by the earthquake of 464 and the helot revolt that followed. When Sparta then sent home the Athenian hoplites Cimon had brought to help against the helots, Athens left the alliance of 481 and allied with Argos, Sparta's enemy.

chapters.title: The empire
chapters.s1: Athens moved the league treasury from Delos to Athens in 454 and from then on spent allied tribute as Athenian revenue, paying jurors, rowers and the builders of the Parthenon.
chapters.s2: The move followed the destruction in 454 of an Athenian expedition sent to Egypt in 460 to support a revolt against Persia, and was justified as security. From 454 one-sixtieth of each payment went to Athena, and the inscribed records of that share are the main evidence for the empire's size: between 150 and 200 tributary cities at most dates. Ephialtes' reform of 461 had already moved power to the council, assembly and courts; Pericles introduced pay for jurors, and in 451 restricted citizenship to children of two Athenian parents, which made the benefits of empire a closed privilege. Allies were required to bring major lawsuits to Athens, and Athenian settlers received land on allied territory. The Parthenon, begun in 447, was paid for in part from the league reserve, and Pericles' opponents said so in the assembly.

chapters.title: Two blocs
chapters.s1: Athens' attempt to add a land empire failed, and the peace of 446-445 recognised two blocs, forbade members to switch sides and held for fifteen years while Sparta's fear of Athenian power grew.
chapters.s2: From 460 Athens fought Corinth, Aegina, Sparta and Thebes while campaigning in Egypt; it won Boeotia at Oenophyta in 457 and lost it at Coronea in 447, and Euboea and Megara revolted in 446. Under the peace Athens gave up its mainland holdings, Megara's ports, Troezen and Achaea, and kept its sea empire; disputes were to go to arbitration. When Samos revolted in 440, Corinth argued in the Peloponnesian League that each bloc had the right to punish its own members, and Sparta stayed out. The arbitration clause decided the next war's blame: Athens offered arbitration in 432, Sparta refused, and Spartans later believed their misfortunes in the war came from that refusal.

stories.today: The Serpent Column, the bronze victory monument for Plataea that lists 31 Greek states, still stands in the Hippodrome in Istanbul, where Constantine moved it. The British Museum holds the Parthenon sculptures removed under Lord Elgin in 1801-1812, and Greece's request for their return remains unresolved.

stories.title: Sicily and Persian Gold
stories.sub: the Peloponnesian War, 433 to 399 BCE
stories.thesis: Athens lost a war its strategy could have drawn: the plague and the Sicilian expedition destroyed its manpower and its reserve, and Persian money then gave Sparta the fleet it could never have paid for on its own.
assumptions: Assumes Pericles' defensive strategy could have produced a peace on acceptable terms; the Peace of Nicias is the evidence, and it held badly.
Assumes Sparta could not have built a fleet without Persia; Syracusan and Corinthian ships after 413 cut against it.
Rests mainly on one witness, an Athenian general exiled in 424 whose account breaks off in 411.
stories.disconfirm: If the thesis were wrong, Athens should have been losing before 415: its revenue, fleet and alliance should have been failing in the first ten years of the war. In 421 Athens held Pylos and 292 Spartan prisoners, had raised the tribute assessment roughly threefold in 425, and lost no major ally except Amphipolis.
stories.awkward: Athens recovered from Sicily. It won at Cyzicus in 410 and at Arginusae in 406, and refused Spartan offers of peace after both, so the war lost in Sicily was still open to a negotiated end in 406 and Athens chose to fight on.

chapters.title: Fear of Athens
chapters.s1: Sparta went to war in 431 out of fear of Athenian power, and it went that year because Corinth threatened to leave the Peloponnesian League if Sparta held back.
chapters.s2: Athens allied in 433 with Corcyra, a Corinthian colony with one of the three largest navies in Greece, and its ships turned back the Corinthian fleet at Sybota. Potidaea, a Corinthian colony paying tribute to Athens, revolted in 432 and was besieged, and the Megarian decree shut Megara out of the harbours of the empire and the Athenian market. At the Spartan assembly of 432 the Corinthians said they would look for other allies; the Spartans voted that Athens had broken the treaty, and the league congress voted for war. Athens offered arbitration under the treaty of 446 and Sparta refused. The war began in spring 431 when Thebes, Sparta's ally, attacked Plataea at night.

chapters.title: The plague
chapters.s1: Pericles' strategy of giving up the countryside and holding the sea assumed Athens could wait out the Spartan invasions; the plague of 430, spreading through a city packed with refugees, killed perhaps a quarter to a third of its people and Pericles with them.
chapters.s2: Spartan King Archidamus II led the Peloponnesian army into Attica each summer while the Athenians, moved inside the walls joining Athens to Piraeus, raided the Peloponnesian coast by sea. The epidemic came in through Piraeus in 430 and killed 4,400 hoplites and 300 cavalrymen among the citizens, more hoplites than Athens lost in any single battle before Sicily. The Athenians fined Pericles and removed him from office in 430, re-elected him, and lost him to the disease in autumn 429. A mass grave of the period excavated in the Kerameikos cemetery was claimed in 2006 to yield typhoid DNA; the identification is disputed. His successors, Cleon above all, preferred offensive war, and the strategy that assumed patience lost its author.

chapters.title: Mytilene and Pylos
chapters.s1: Without Pericles Athens fought harder and with more luck: it held its allies by terror after Mytilene's revolt and captured 292 Spartans at Pylos in 425, the best bargaining counter of the war.
chapters.s2: Mytilene, one of the last allies still supplying ships, revolted in 428; the assembly voted to kill every adult male, reversed the vote the next day after the speaker Diodotus argued from Athenian interest, and the second trireme arrived just in time; more than a thousand ringleaders were executed. In 427 Sparta took Plataea after a two-year siege and killed its defenders. In 425 the general Demosthenes fortified Pylos on the Messenian coast and cut off 420 Spartans on the island of Sphacteria; Cleon brought 292 back, about 120 of them Spartiates, and the threat to kill them ended the invasions of Attica. Sparta answered through Brasidas, who took Amphipolis in 424, and the Athenian general who lost it was exiled for twenty years and used them to write the war's history. Cleon and Brasidas both died at Amphipolis in 422, and the Peace of Nicias in 421 restored prewar positions.

chapters.title: Melos and Sicily
chapters.s1: The peace never settled the war, and in 415 Athens sent its largest expedition to conquer Syracuse; by 413 it had lost two fleets, two armies and its reserve.
chapters.s2: In the winter of 416-415 Athens killed the men of the neutral island of Melos and enslaved the women and children for refusing to join the empire. Alcibiades proposed the Sicilian venture on an appeal from Segesta; Nicias opposed it and inflated the request, and the assembly granted 134 triremes and 5,100 hoplites. Days before sailing the city's herms were mutilated, Alcibiades was recalled to stand trial, and he fled to Sparta, where he advised sending the Spartan Gylippus to Syracuse and fortifying Decelea in Attica. Decelea cost Athens its Laurion silver and more than 20,000 runaway slaves. A second fleet of 73 triremes failed to turn the siege, and in 413 the army was destroyed on its retreat, Nicias and Demosthenes were executed, and 7,000 prisoners went to the stone quarries of Syracuse, where some reportedly won release by reciting Athenian tragedy.

chapters.title: Persian money
chapters.s1: The Sicilian disaster brought Persia back into the Aegean: from 412 its governors paid Sparta's rowers in return for the Greek cities of Asia, and the partnership of Cyrus the Younger and Lysander from 407 made the payments decisive.
chapters.s2: The satraps Tissaphernes and Pharnabazus competed to fund Sparta, and three treaties in 412-411 recognised the King's claim to the Asian Greek cities, the freedom Sparta had gone to war to defend. Chios, Miletus and much of Ionia revolted from Athens in 412. At Athens an oligarchic coup in 411 set up the Four Hundred on the promise that Persia would fund an oligarchy; the fleet at Samos stayed democratic and recalled Alcibiades. Athens destroyed a Spartan fleet at Cyzicus in 410 and won at Arginusae in 406, refused Spartan peace offers both times, and after Arginusae executed six of its generals for failing to rescue men in a storm. Persia rebuilt Sparta's fleet each time, and Cyrus, sent west by his father Darius II, raised Spartan pay from three obols a day to four, which drew rowers away from Athenian ships.

chapters.title: Aegospotami
chapters.s1: Lysander's Persian-paid fleet caught the Athenian fleet beached at Aegospotami in 405 and took it almost whole, and Athens, cut off from Black Sea grain, surrendered in April 404.
chapters.s2: The Athenian fleet of 180 ships lay on an open beach across the Hellespont from Lysander's base at Lampsacus; Lysander attacked when the crews were ashore for food, and only about twelve ships escaped, among them the general Conon's. Lysander executed the Athenian prisoners, about 3,000 by one account, and blockaded Piraeus. Corinth and Thebes wanted Athens destroyed and its people enslaved; Sparta refused, citing Athens' service against Persia and wanting a counterweight to Thebes. The terms: the Long Walls and the walls of Piraeus pulled down, all but twelve ships surrendered, the exiles recalled, and Athens to follow Sparta in war and peace. The walls came down to the music of flute girls, and the victors called it the first day of Greek freedom.

chapters.title: The Thirty
chapters.s1: Sparta's victory produced a Spartan-backed junta at Athens that killed about 1,500 citizens in eight months and fell in 403, and the democracy restored after it proved more stable than the empire it had lost.
chapters.s2: Lysander installed the Thirty under Critias with a Spartan garrison on the Acropolis; they limited full citizenship to 3,000, executed resident foreigners for their property and put to death their own moderate member Theramenes. Exiles under Thrasybulus seized the border fort of Phyle and then Piraeus. Spartan King Pausanias, distrusting Lysander, brokered a settlement in 403 with an amnesty that bound Athenians not to recall past wrongs, and the democracy repaid from public funds the loan the Thirty had taken from Sparta to fight it. The restored democracy lasted until the Macedonian settlement of 322. Its most disputed act was the trial of Socrates in 399, the teacher of Critias and Alcibiades, condemned for impiety and corrupting the young.

stories.today: The war's contemporary history is a set text at the US Naval War College and other staff colleges, and its claim that Spartan fear of Athens' growth made war inevitable is the ancient analogy most often cited in the debate over US-China rivalry. The amnesty of 403, which barred prosecutions for acts committed under the Thirty, is the earliest well-documented political amnesty and a standard case in the study of transitional justice.

stories.title: Freedom by Decree
stories.sub: from Spartan hegemony to the sack of Corinth, 404 to 146 BCE
stories.thesis: After 404 no Greek city could lead the others without an outside sponsor, and from the King's Peace of 387 to the sack of Corinth in 146 the 'freedom of the Greeks' was a grant made by Persia, Macedon and Rome that kept the cities divided.
assumptions: Assumes Macedon won through money and a professional army more than through Greek decline; the Greek cities were as populous and rich in the 4th century as in the 5th.
Assumes the Hellenistic kingdoms belong in a Greek story; most of their subjects were Egyptians, Syrians, Babylonians and Iranians.
Assumes Rome's eastern wars were reactive until 168; a rival reading has Rome seeking dominance in Greece from 200.
stories.disconfirm: If the thesis were wrong, a Greek power should have led Greece without an outside sponsor for a generation after 404. Thebes is the test: it won at Leuctra in 371 without Persian money and dominated the Peloponnese for nine years, sought Persian backing in 367 and was refused by the Greeks, and lost its leadership when Epaminondas died in 362.
stories.awkward: Losing the freedom to make war left the polis intact as a working community: Greek cities ran their own courts, festivals and finances under the kings and Rome for six more centuries, and Alexander and his successors founded more Greek cities than the archaic colonists had.

chapters.title: The King's Peace
chapters.s1: Sparta's hegemony after 404 depended on Persia, and when Sparta invaded Persian Asia Minor, Persian money raised a Greek coalition against it until Sparta accepted a peace the Persian King dictated in 387.
chapters.s2: Lysander replaced the Athenian empire with Spartan governors and boards of ten local partisans, and Sparta backed Cyrus the Younger's bid for the Persian throne. About 13,000 Greek mercenaries fought for Cyrus at Cunaxa near Babylon in 401; he was killed, and the survivors, the Ten Thousand, marched out through Armenia to the Black Sea. Spartan King Agesilaus II campaigned in Asia from 396 until Persian gold paid Thebes, Athens, Corinth and Argos to start the Corinthian War in 395; the Persian coin, the daric, bore an archer, and Agesilaus said Persian archers had driven him from Asia. The King's Peace gave the Asian Greek cities and Cyprus to Persia and declared all other cities autonomous, with Sparta as its enforcer. Sparta used the autonomy clause to dissolve the Boeotian League and in 382 seized the Cadmea, the citadel of Thebes, in peacetime.

chapters.title: Leuctra
chapters.s1: Thebes broke Spartan power at Leuctra in 371 and freed Messenia in 369, which ended the helot economy that had made Sparta possible, and then failed to build a lasting order in its place.
chapters.s2: Theban exiles expelled the Spartan garrison in 379, and in 378 Athens founded a new league whose charter promised members freedom from tribute, garrisons and governors, the abuses of its first empire listed as prohibitions. At Leuctra the Boeotarch Epaminondas massed his left wing fifty shields deep against the Spartan right and killed King Cleombrotus I and about 400 of the 700 Spartiates present; Sparta's citizen body, perhaps 8,000 in 480, had fallen to under 1,500 and could not replace them. Theban armies invaded Laconia in 370-369, freed the helots of Messenia, founded the city of Messene on Mount Ithome and backed a new Arcadian League. In 367 the Theban general Pelopidas obtained a Persian rescript in Thebes' favour, and the Greek cities refused to swear to it. Epaminondas died winning at Mantinea in 362, and a contemporary wrote that the battle left Greece in more confusion and disorder than before.

chapters.title: Philip
chapters.s1: Philip II took Macedon in collapse in 359 and, with Pangaion gold and a professional army, made himself master of Greece at Chaeronea in 338, while the cities able to stop him were spent from fighting each other.
chapters.s2: Philip became king after his brother Perdiccas III died with 4,000 men fighting the Illyrians; he had spent about three years as a hostage in Thebes, the city of Epaminondas. He armed Macedonian farmers with the sarissa, a pike about five metres long, and drilled them as a standing phalanx, and the mines at Crenides, taken in 356 and renamed Philippi, gave him more than 1,000 talents a year. Athens lost Chios, Rhodes, Cos and Byzantium in the Social War of 357-355 as Philip took Amphipolis and the north Aegean coast; he razed Olynthus in 348, and the peace of 346 gave him a seat on the council of Delphi. At Chaeronea in August 338 the Macedonian army beat Athens and Thebes; the Theban Sacred Band died almost to a man, and 254 skeletons were found under the stone lion raised over their grave. In 337 Philip made the Greek states swear a common peace, the League of Corinth, with himself as its leader, a ban on overthrowing existing constitutions and a declared war of revenge on Persia.

chapters.title: Alexander
chapters.s1: Alexander used the league's war of revenge to destroy the Persian Empire in four years, and moved the centre of the Greek world from the Aegean cities to the courts of kings in Egypt and Asia.
chapters.s2: Philip was murdered at Aegae in 336; when Thebes revolted in 335 Alexander razed it and sold about 30,000 Thebans into slavery. He crossed to Asia in 334 with about 37,000 men, won at the Granicus that year, beat Darius III at Issus in 333, took Tyre after a seven-month siege in 332, founded Alexandria in Egypt and destroyed the Persian army at Gaugamela in October 331. More Greeks fought for Persia than for Alexander in the early battles: at the Granicus he massacred the Greek mercenaries in Persian service and sent 2,000 survivors to Macedon in chains. Persepolis was burned in 330, and the Persian treasuries yielded about 180,000 talents of bullion, which Alexander and his successors coined and spent across the eastern Mediterranean. He reached the Hydaspes in the Punjab in 326, where his army refused to go further, and died at Babylon in 323.

chapters.title: The kingdoms
chapters.s1: Alexander died without an adult heir, and twenty years of war among his generals ended at Ipsus in 301 with the empire divided among kings who treated the old cities as prizes and proclaimed their freedom when it served.
chapters.s2: Athens led a Greek revolt at the news of his death and lost it at Crannon and off Amorgos in 322; the regent Antipater restricted citizenship to men worth 2,000 drachmas, cutting the citizen body from 21,000 to 9,000, and put a garrison in the Piraeus. In 315 Antigonus the One-Eyed declared at Tyre that all Greeks should be free, ungarrisoned and autonomous, and his rivals answered with the same promise. At Ipsus in 301 Seleucus, Lysimachus and Cassander killed Antigonus; Seleucus' war elephants, obtained from the Indian emperor Chandragupta Maurya in exchange for the eastern satrapies, decided the battle. Antigonid Macedon, Seleucid Asia and Ptolemaic Egypt then held the field for a century. The cities' own answer was federation: the Achaean League, refounded in 281, took Corinth's citadel from its Macedonian garrison in 243 and grew to include most of the Peloponnese.

chapters.title: Rome's grant
chapters.s1: Rome entered Greece to stop Philip V's alliance with Hannibal and stayed to arbitrate it: at the Isthmian Games of 196 the Roman commander Titus Quinctius Flamininus proclaimed the Greeks free, and the cities found that freedom granted by Rome meant deferring to Rome.
chapters.s2: At the peace conference of Naupactus in 217 an Aetolian delegate warned the Greeks to settle their quarrels before the cloud gathering in the west, the war between Rome and Carthage, settled on Greece. Philip V of Macedon allied with Hannibal in 215 after Cannae, and Rome fought him in 214-205 and again from 200 until its legions broke his phalanx at Cynoscephalae in 197. The proclamation at the Isthmus freed the cities Philip had held, and the crowd's shout was said to have brought down birds flying overhead. Rome withdrew its troops in 194 and returned within three years to expel the Seleucid king Antiochus III from Greece, and after his defeat at Magnesia in 190 the treaty of Apamea pushed Seleucid power beyond the Taurus mountains. From then on Greek disputes went to the Senate, and every faction in every city sought a Roman patron.

chapters.title: Corinth
chapters.s1: Rome's tolerance of Greek freedom ended in 168, when it abolished the Macedonian monarchy after Pydna, and in 146 it razed Corinth and broke up the Achaean League, the last independent Greek power.
chapters.s2: After King Perseus lost at Pydna in 168, Rome split Macedon into four republics, took 1,000 leading Achaeans to Italy as hostages, and in 167 enslaved some 150,000 people in Epirus. The same summer the Roman envoy Gaius Popillius Laenas drew a circle in the sand round the Seleucid king Antiochus IV outside Alexandria and told him to answer the Senate's demand to leave Egypt before stepping out of it; Antiochus left. A pretender's revolt in 149-148 made Macedonia a Roman province. When Rome ordered the Achaean League to release Sparta, Corinth and Argos, the league went to war, and the consul Lucius Mummius destroyed Corinth in 146, killed its men and sold its women and children. Mummius shipped Corinth's paintings and statues to Rome and is said to have warned the shippers that anything they lost would have to be replaced with new ones.

stories.today: Alexandria, founded in 331, is Egypt's second city, and several cities from Central Asia to Afghanistan trace their names or origins to Alexander's foundations. The Achaean League was studied by the authors of the US Constitution: Federalist No. 18 uses it as an example of a confederacy that failed for want of central authority.

arc.title: Faith Follows Power
arc.sub: Judaism, Christianity and Islam as political events, c. 925 BCE to 750 CE
arc.thesis: Each of the three monotheisms took its lasting form from a political turn, Judaism from the loss of its state, Christianity from its capture of the Roman one and Islam from building its own, so that each faith's defining texts and divisions date from those turns more than from its founding teaching.
assumptions: Assumes the forms that lasted (rabbinic Judaism, Nicene and Chalcedonian Christianity, Sunni and Shia Islam) are the right end-points; believers measure each faith by fidelity to revelation, which history cannot test.
Assumes political and religious motives can be separated for analysis; the Maccabees, the martyrs and the first caliphs drew no such line.

Assumes the narrative sources, most written by the winning party and often generations after the events, report the political sequence well enough to be tested against inscriptions, papyri, coins and outside chronicles.
arc.disconfirm: If the thesis were wrong, the defining texts and doctrines would be fixed before the political turns: a Torah complete under the kings, a Nicene consensus that held without emperors, a Sunni-Shia division over doctrine from its first day. Christianity's growth is the strongest test, since it went from a few thousand followers to perhaps a tenth of the Roman population by 300 with no state behind it.
arc.awkward: The Church of the East kept a Nicene creed with no Christian state behind it, organised in 410 under a Zoroastrian shah, and its missionary Alopen reached the Tang capital Chang'an in 635; the widest missionary reach of the period belonged to the one major church that never held power.

stories.title: Law Without a State
stories.sub: Israel, Judah and the making of rabbinic Judaism, c. 925 BCE to 500 CE
stories.thesis: Judaism became a religion able to outlive its state because each destruction, by Assyria in 722 BCE, Babylon in 587 BCE and Rome in 70 and 135 CE, moved authority from king and Temple toward a written law and the scholars who interpreted it.
assumptions: Assumes the biblical histories, written largely in Judah from the late seventh century BCE and revised in exile, give their authors' views, checkable against Assyrian, Babylonian and Persian records where they overlap.
Assumes the rabbinic line is the one to follow; the Samaritans, the Elephantine garrison and the Qumran community were also Israelite answers, and only the Samaritans survive, in small numbers.
stories.disconfirm: If the thesis were wrong, the text-centred religion would be visible before the losses: a complete Torah under the monarchy, or scholars governing Jewish life while kings and Temple stood. Josiah's reform of about 622 BCE is the test, since it put a book at the centre of worship 35 years before the first Temple fell.
stories.awkward: A century after the return from Babylon, the Jewish garrison at Elephantine on the Nile kept its own temple to Yahu, invoked Anat-Yahu and other gods beside him, and in 407 BCE petitioned the Persian governor of Judah and the sons of Samaria's governor for help rebuilding it; exile had produced no single law observed everywhere.

chapters.title: Judah alone
chapters.s1: Assyria's destruction of the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 BCE left Judah, the smaller and poorer of two Yahweh-worshipping states, as the sole heir of their traditions.
chapters.s2: Israel was the stronger kingdom for two centuries: its King Ahab fielded 2,000 chariots against the Assyrian King Shalmaneser III at Qarqar in 853 BCE, and King Mesha of Moab named its King Omri and its god Yahweh on a stele around 840 BCE, the earliest certain reference to Yahweh outside the Bible. The outside evidence for Judah is thinner: Pharaoh Shoshenq I's list of towns raided around 925 BCE names Megiddo and omits Jerusalem, and the only near-contemporary trace of David is the phrase read as 'House of David' on an Aramaean stele from Tel Dan. Assyria under Tiglath-Pileser III turned tribute into annexation, and Shalmaneser V and Sargon II took Samaria after a three-year siege, Sargon recording 27,290 deportees. Refugees went south, and Jerusalem's walled area expanded sharply in the late eighth century, the material basis for Judah's later claim to speak for all Israel. The Assyrian King Sennacherib took Lachish and, by his own count, 46 Judean towns in 701 BCE, but left Jerusalem standing under King Hezekiah for 30 talents of gold and 800 of silver.

chapters.title: The book in the Temple
chapters.s1: With Assyria in retreat, King Josiah of Judah centralised worship in Jerusalem around a written law, the first time a book was made the authority over Israelite religion.
chapters.s2: The scroll the priest Hilkiah reported finding in the Temple around 622 BCE is identified by most scholars with a core of Deuteronomy, and the reform it licensed served the crown: rural shrines were closed, the old northern sanctuary at Bethel was desecrated, and sacrifice was confined to the capital the king controlled. Assyria's collapse made the programme possible, and the Medes and Babylonians sacked Nineveh in 612 BCE, leaving the Levant without a master. Josiah's freedom of action lasted thirteen years. Pharaoh Necho II, marching north to join the last Assyrian forces, killed him at Megiddo in 609 BCE, and the Babylonian Crown Prince Nebuchadnezzar destroyed the Egyptian army at Carchemish in 605 BCE, making Judah a Babylonian vassal. The reform's lasting product was a history: the books from Joshua to Kings judge every king by whether he centralised worship, and their first edition is widely dated to Josiah's court.

chapters.title: Exile
chapters.s1: Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple in 587 BCE and deported its elite, and the deportees, rather than those left in Judah, wrote the version of the religion that survived.
chapters.s2: King Nebuchadnezzar II first took Jerusalem in March 597 BCE, deporting King Jehoiachin with the court and craftsmen, and returned in 587 BCE after the vassal King Zedekiah rebelled. Babylonian ration tablets list Jehoiachin, 'king of Judah', drawing oil at the Babylonian court, a rare outside confirmation of the biblical account. The exiles kept their identity through practices that needed no Temple, circumcision, the Sabbath and food rules, and through editing the texts of the prophets and the law. The Persian King Cyrus II took Babylon in 539 BCE and let the deportees return, a policy he applied to other peoples' cults as well, which is why the book of Isaiah calls him the Lord's anointed. Most exiles stayed, and Babylonia remained a centre of Jewish learning until the eleventh century CE.

chapters.title: Temple and Torah
chapters.s1: Under Persian rule Judah became a small temple-province governed by priests and Persian appointees, and in that setting the Torah was assembled and made the province's law.
chapters.s2: The Second Temple was dedicated in 516 BCE under King Darius I, in a province of Yehud whose population is estimated in the tens of thousands at most, around a Jerusalem far smaller than the city Babylon had burned. Nehemiah, a Jewish official at the court of Artaxerxes I, came as governor in 445 BCE and rebuilt the walls in 52 days against the opposition of Sanballat, governor of Samaria. The scribe Ezra, dated either to 458 or to 398 BCE, is credited in the biblical account with reading the law of Moses to an assembly that bound itself to keep it; most scholars place the final compilation of the five books in this period, and Persian authorisation of local law codes is one plausible spur. The Elephantine papyri show how incomplete the process was at the edges, with a Jewish garrison on the Nile keeping its own temple to Yahu until 410 BCE.

chapters.title: The Maccabees
chapters.s1: Greek rule split Judea over assimilation, and the revolt it provoked restored a Jewish state that used its power to impose Judaism on its neighbours.
chapters.s2: The Torah was translated into Greek at Alexandria in the third century BCE for a diaspora that no longer read Hebrew, the version later adopted as the church's Old Testament. The Seleucid King Antiochus III won Judea from the Ptolemies at Panium in 200 BCE; his son Antiochus IV, backing a Hellenising party in Jerusalem, banned circumcision and the Sabbath and set a pagan altar in the Temple in 167 BCE. The revolt led by the priest Mattathias and his son Judah Maccabee retook the Temple in 164 BCE, and in 141 BCE an assembly in Jerusalem made Judah's brother Simon high priest and ruler, with Seleucid dynastic wars doing as much as Jewish arms to make independence hold. The Hasmonean state then expanded by conquest: John Hyrcanus I made the Idumeans convert and destroyed the Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim, which excavation dates to about 111 BCE. The Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes appear in the sources in these Hasmonean decades as rival answers to who should interpret the law under a priest-king.

chapters.title: Rome
chapters.s1: A Hasmonean succession war invited Rome in, and Roman rule, first through clients and then directly, ended in a revolt that destroyed the Second Temple in 70 CE.
chapters.s2: The Roman general Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BCE after the brothers Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II both appealed to him, and entered the Holy of Holies. The Senate made Herod, an Idumean from a family converted under the Hasmoneans, king of Judea; he took Jerusalem in 37 BCE and from about 20 BCE rebuilt the Temple as one of the largest sanctuaries in the Roman world. Rome annexed Judea as a province in 6 CE, and the census that followed provoked the first armed rejection of Roman taxation. The war of 66 began after the governor Gessius Florus took 17 talents from the Temple treasury and Greeks and Jews clashed at Caesarea; rebels then destroyed a Syrian legionary column at the Beth Horon pass, which committed Rome to full reconquest. Titus took Jerusalem in the summer of 70, and Rome diverted the tax every Jew had paid to the Temple to the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus in Rome.

chapters.title: The rabbis
chapters.s1: With the Temple gone and a second revolt crushed, authority passed to rabbis who codified the law in the Mishnah around 200 CE, and Judaism became a religion of study that needed no state.
chapters.s2: Rabbinic tradition has the sage Yohanan ben Zakkai smuggled out of besieged Jerusalem in a coffin to obtain from the general Vespasian leave to teach at Yavneh, which became the centre where the calendar and liturgy were rebuilt without sacrifice. Simon bar Kokhba's revolt of 132 to 136, provoked by Emperor Hadrian's refounding of Jerusalem as the colony Aelia Capitolina, ended with Judea depopulated, Jews barred from the city and the province renamed Syria Palaestina. The rabbinic movement moved north to Galilee, where the patriarch Judah ha-Nasi compiled the Mishnah's six orders, a code that legislates in detail for Temple sacrifice more than a century after the last one. The Christian empire let the patriarchate lapse after Gamaliel VI died in 425 and diverted its revenues to the treasury. The centre of gravity moved to Babylonia under Persian rule, where the academies of Sura and Pumbedita brought the Babylonian Talmud to its final form by the sixth century.

stories.today: About 15.7 million people identified as Jewish in 2024, nearly half of them in Israel, the first Jewish state since the Hasmoneans. Jewish law is still taught from the Mishnah and the Babylonian Talmud, and the fast of the Ninth of Av still mourns the Temple's destructions in 587 BCE and 70 CE.

stories.title: The Imperial Church
stories.sub: from Jewish sect to state religion and schism, c. 30 to 635 CE
stories.thesis: Christianity grew to a tenth of the Roman Empire without state support, but it became a single, enforced orthodoxy only when emperors took up its disputes, and the same imperial machinery that defined the faith at Nicaea and Chalcedon broke it apart in the provinces that refused the definitions.
assumptions: Assumes the doctrinal disputes were real disagreements that politics adjudicated, and more than cover for regional and personal rivalries.
Assumes the councils' decisions mattered more than what ordinary believers held, about which the evidence is thin before the fifth century.
Assumes the population estimates, about a tenth of the empire Christian by 300, are roughly right; they rest on extrapolation from scattered evidence.
stories.disconfirm: If the thesis were wrong, Nicene orthodoxy should have prevailed without imperial backing. The test is 337 to 378, when Emperors Constantius II and Valens backed bishops who rejected Nicaea's formula: Nicene Christianity survived those decades in Egypt and the West, but it became the empire's single creed only through Theodosius I's law of 380 and his council of 381.
stories.awkward: The growth that made Constantine's choice worth making owed nothing to the state: after three centuries of intermittent persecution, Christians were perhaps a tenth of the empire's population by 300, concentrated in the cities and the Greek-speaking East.
