chapters.title: A Jewish sect
chapters.s1: The Roman prefect Pontius Pilate crucified Jesus of Nazareth around 30 CE as a threat to order, and his followers' claim that he had risen kept a Jewish messianic movement alive after its leader's death.
chapters.s2: Jesus preached in Galilee, ruled by Herod's son Antipas, and was executed in Judea, under direct Roman rule since 6 CE, on a charge the Gospels give as claiming to be king of the Jews; crucifixion was Rome's penalty for rebels and slaves. A stone found at Caesarea in 1961 names Pilate as prefect of Judea, the only inscription of his rule. His first followers were Jews who kept the Temple and the law in Jerusalem under his brother James and expected his return within their lifetimes. The earliest written evidence is the letters of Paul of Tarsus, a Pharisee who had persecuted the movement and joined it a few years after the crucifixion following a vision near Damascus; the letters predate every Gospel.

chapters.title: The gentile mission
chapters.s1: Paul's mission admitted gentiles without circumcision, terms the Jerusalem leaders accepted around 49 CE, and it turned a Jewish sect into a religion open to the whole Roman world.
chapters.s2: The meeting of Paul and Barnabas with James, Peter and John set the terms: gentile converts kept a short list of food and sexual rules and were spared circumcision and the rest of the law. Paul then founded churches in the Greek cities of Asia Minor, Macedonia and Greece and wrote the letters that are the oldest Christian documents. The Roman state first noticed the movement as a Jewish disturbance: Emperor Claudius expelled Jews from Rome, in 49 CE by one later account, after riots a Roman biographer attributed to one 'Chrestus'. Emperor Nero blamed Rome's Christians for the fire of July 64, by which time they were distinct enough from the Jews to be singled out. The Temple's destruction in 70 removed the Jerusalem church's base, and by the end of the century the movement's centre of gravity was gentile and urban.

chapters.title: Persecution
chapters.s1: For two centuries persecution was local and sporadic; it became imperial policy when emperors facing military and fiscal crisis demanded proof of loyalty to the gods, and the church came through it larger.
chapters.s2: Emperor Trajan's reply to Pliny, governor of Bithynia, around 112 set the early rule: Christians were not to be sought out and anonymous accusations were to be ignored, but those who confessed and refused to sacrifice were executed. Emperor Decius, after sacrificing to Jupiter on 3 January 250, ordered every inhabitant to sacrifice and obtain a signed certificate, a libellus, of which dozens survive on papyrus from Egypt; Bishop Fabian of Rome was among those killed. The edict lapsed with Decius' death in 251, but the quarrel over readmitting the many who had complied divided the church, and the same question returned after the next persecution as the Donatist schism in North Africa. Emperor Gallienus restored church property in 260, a tacit recognition that the church could own it. The Great Persecution opened on 24 February 303 with the razing of the church at Nicomedia and ended in the East with Emperor Galerius' edict of toleration in April 311, an admission that coercion had failed.

chapters.title: Constantine
chapters.s1: Emperor Constantine I adopted Christianity after his victory at the Milvian Bridge in 312 and at once made himself arbiter of its disputes, the origin of state-defined orthodoxy.
chapters.s2: Constantine and his co-emperor Licinius agreed at Milan in February 313 to tolerate all cults and return confiscated church property; Constantine went further, exempting clergy from civic duties and funding churches, among them the Lateran basilica in Rome. Within two years he was adjudicating the Donatist dispute in Africa, referring it to the Council of Arles in 314 and enforcing the verdict with confiscations. He summoned the Council of Nicaea in 325 to settle the dispute over the Alexandrian priest Arius, and the bishops' creed, with its term homoousios, 'of one substance', came with imperial exile for those who refused it. He dedicated Constantinople as a second capital in 330, and King Ezana of Aksum adopted Christianity in the same decade. Constantine was baptised only on his deathbed in 337, by Bishop Eusebius of Nicomedia, a sympathiser of Arius.

chapters.title: One lawful faith
chapters.s1: Fifty years of imperial wavering between Nicene and anti-Nicene bishops ended when Emperor Theodosius I made Nicene Christianity the only lawful faith in 380 and enforced it against heretics and pagans.
chapters.s2: Constantine's son Constantius II and later Emperor Valens backed bishops who rejected Nicaea's formula, and Ulfilas, made bishop of the Goths around 341 by that party, gave the Goths a Gothic Bible and an anti-Nicene Christianity they kept for two centuries. Emperor Julian, sole ruler from 361 to 363, reopened the temples, barred Christians from teaching the classics and authorised the rebuilding of the Jerusalem Temple, which stopped when fire broke out at the foundations; his death on campaign in Persia ended the last pagan reign. Theodosius' edict of February 380 defined the lawful faith as that of the bishops of Rome and Alexandria, and his council at Constantinople in 381, with no Western bishops present, extended the Nicene creed to the form churches recite today and ranked Constantinople second after Rome. Laws of 391 closed the temples, and in Alexandria soldiers and Christians destroyed the Serapeum, the city's great temple of Serapis.

chapters.title: Two cities
chapters.s1: As the Western empire failed, Bishop Augustine of Hippo gave the Latin church a theology that detached Christianity's fate from Rome's while keeping the state's coercive power at the church's service.
chapters.s2: Alaric's Visigoths sacked Rome in August 410, and pagans blamed the abandonment of the old gods; Augustine answered in the City of God, written from 413 to 426, which treats every earthly state, Rome included, as passing and the community of the saved as the only lasting city. In the same years he argued for coercing the Donatists, the North African church that had refused bishops tainted by the Great Persecution, and at the Carthage hearing of 411 the imperial commissioner Marcellinus ruled against them and the state took their churches. Augustine's reading of the parable's 'compel them to come in' became the Latin church's standing justification for using state force against heretics. The Vandals were besieging Hippo when he died in 430, and the Western empire was gone by 476. The Frankish King Clovis' Catholic baptism around 496, when most Germanic kings were anti-Nicene, gave the Roman church its chief lay protector in the West.

chapters.title: The broken church
chapters.s1: In the East the emperors' councils defined Christ's nature at Ephesus in 431 and Chalcedon in 451, and the provinces that rejected the definitions built their own churches, which emperors could neither persuade nor coerce back.
chapters.s2: The church in Persia, organised at Seleucia-Ctesiphon in 410 under Shah Yazdegerd I, followed the theology Ephesus condemned, and the Church of the East it became sent the missionary Alopen to the Tang capital Chang'an in 635. Chalcedon's formula of one person in two natures held in Rome and Constantinople and was rejected by most Christians in Egypt and much of Syria and Armenia, who confessed one incarnate nature. Emperor Zeno's Henotikon of 482, a compromise issued without a council, failed in the East and split Constantinople from Rome until 519. Empress Theodora's protection allowed Jacob Baradaeus to be consecrated bishop of Edessa in 543 or 544 and to ordain a separate hierarchy across Syria, Anatolia and Egypt, and the Syriac Orthodox church was long called Jacobite after him. When the Arabs reached Egypt in 639, the Coptic Patriarch Benjamin had spent most of a decade in hiding from Cyrus, the Chalcedonian patriarch the emperor had also made governor, and the Arab commander Amr ibn al-As restored him.

stories.today: About 2.3 billion people were Christian in 2020. The creed as extended at Constantinople in 381 is recited by Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant churches, while the Coptic, Syriac, Armenian and Ethiopian churches that rejected Chalcedon in 451, and the Assyrian Church of the East, remain separate communions.

stories.title: Who Should Rule
stories.sub: Arabia, Muhammad and the caliphate, c. 570 to 750 CE
stories.thesis: Islam was a state as well as a faith from Muhammad's arrival at Medina in 622, and its lasting divisions began as disputes over who should rule that state, with the doctrines that now separate Sunni and Shia elaborated afterwards to justify the political sides.
assumptions: Assumes the outline of Muhammad's life in the biographies, the earliest surviving in a ninth-century edition, is broadly reliable where it agrees with the Quran, the Medina agreement and non-Muslim sources from the 630s.
Assumes the conquests were driven by the new state's need to direct tribal manpower and pay it from tribute, with religion as the bond; the sources allow a more devotional reading.
Assumes Sunni and Shia are the right end-points; both took settled doctrinal form only in the eighth and ninth centuries.
stories.disconfirm: If the thesis were wrong, the Sunni-Shia division would rest on a doctrinal difference visible from the start, or the conquests would have sought converts. The conversion evidence points one way: the conquerors settled in garrison cities, taxed non-Muslims and, under the Umayyads, kept taxing many converts. The designation of Ali at Ghadir Khumm is the harder case, since Shia tradition holds that the dispute was doctrinal from the Prophet's death.
stories.awkward: Shi'ism drew its strength from losing: Husayn's small force was destroyed at Karbala in 680, the movement grew for seventy years in opposition, and the Abbasids who used Karbala's memory to take power in 750 then kept the caliphate from Ali's descendants.

chapters.title: Arabia between empires
chapters.s1: The last war between Rome and Persia, fought from 602 to 628, exhausted both empires and dismantled the Arab client system that had kept the peninsula's frontiers in order.
chapters.s2: Persia had taken Yemen from Aksum's proxies in the 570s, so that in Muhammad's youth the great powers held both ends of Arabia's caravan trade. Shah Khosrow II executed the Lakhmid King al-Nu'man III in 602 and ruled the desert frontier directly, and Arab tribes soon defeated a Persian force at Dhi Qar; Rome had broken up its own Ghassanid client federation in the 580s. Persian armies took Jerusalem in 614, carried the True Cross to Ctesiphon and occupied Egypt, until Emperor Heraclius invaded Mesopotamia and destroyed the Persian field army near Nineveh in December 627. Khosrow was overthrown and killed, and Persia fell into a succession crisis. The Quran's thirtieth sura opens with the Romans defeated 'in the nearest land' and foretells their victory within a few years, evidence that Muhammad's hearers followed the war closely.

chapters.title: Medina
chapters.s1: Muhammad's move from Mecca to Medina in 622 turned a persecuted preacher into the arbiter of a town, and the community he led there was a polity with its own law, alliances and wars from its first years.
chapters.s2: Muhammad, a Meccan merchant of the Quraysh tribe's Hashim clan, preached from the revelations Muslims date to 610; Mecca's leaders resisted a message that condemned the gods whose shrine drew pilgrims and trade. The feuding clans of Medina invited him as arbiter, and the agreement known as the Constitution of Medina made the emigrants, the Medinans and named Jewish groups one community, an umma, with disputes referred to God and Muhammad. The Muslim calendar counts from the hijra, a choice made under Caliph Umar I around 638, which dates the faith from the founding of the polity rather than from the first revelation. At Badr in March 624 some 313 Muslims defeated a larger Meccan force and killed its leader Abu Jahl, and raids on Meccan caravans became both the polity's economy and its proof of divine favour. Medina's three main Jewish clans were expelled or, in the case of the Qurayza after the siege of 627, put to death by the biographers' account.

chapters.title: Mecca and the succession
chapters.s1: Muhammad took Mecca in 630 by negotiation backed by force, and when he died two years later the community's first decision was political: who would lead the state he had built.
chapters.s2: The truce of Hudaybiyya in March 628 treated Medina as Mecca's equal, and when Mecca's allies broke it Muhammad marched with some 10,000 men and entered the city in January 630 with little fighting. He cleared the Kaaba's idols and kept the shrine, making Mecca's sanctuary Islam's centre and its leading clans, the Umayyads among them, part of the new order. Muhammad died in June 632 without a settled succession; at the Saqifa hall the Medinans proposed a leader of their own, and Abu Bakr was chosen while Ali, the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, was preparing the body for burial. Shia tradition holds that Muhammad had designated Ali at Ghadir Khumm months earlier, and Sunni tradition that he left the choice to the community. Abu Bakr's first act was war against tribes that had stopped paying alms to Medina and against rival prophets such as Musaylima, killed at Yamama in December 632; by March 633 Arabia was united under one authority for the first time.

chapters.title: The conquests
chapters.s1: The state Abu Bakr had united by force turned outward, and within fifteen years Arab armies took Syria, Iraq, Egypt and most of Iran from two empires that had just fought each other to exhaustion.
chapters.s2: Arab forces destroyed the Roman army of Syria at the Yarmuk in 636 and a Persian army at Qadisiyya soon after, and Caliph Umar received Jerusalem's surrender in person from the Patriarch Sophronius and let Jews live in the city again. Amr ibn al-As took Egypt between 639 and 642 among a population mostly hostile to the Chalcedonian church of Constantinople, and founded Fustat as a garrison town. Nahavand in 642 ended organised Persian resistance, and the last shah, Yazdegerd III, was killed near Merv in 651. The conquerors settled in garrison cities such as Kufa, Basra and Fustat, paid from registers of tribute, and made little effort to convert subjects, who remained the majority in most provinces for two centuries or more. Caliph Uthman's standard text of the Quran, copied around 650 and sent to the garrison cities with orders to burn variant codices, was an act of state that fixed the scripture of a dispersed army.

chapters.title: The first civil war
chapters.s1: The conquests' spoils turned the succession question into civil war, and Caliph Uthman's murder in 656 began a five-year struggle that fixed the lines of Islam's lasting divisions.
chapters.s2: Uthman, of the Umayyad clan, was accused of favouring kinsmen with governorships and conquered land, and rebels from Egypt and Iraq killed him in Medina in June 656. Ali became caliph and defeated the Prophet's widow Aisha and the companions Talha and Zubayr near Basra in December 656, the first battle between Muslim armies. Mu'awiya, Uthman's kinsman and governor of Syria, refused allegiance; at Siffin in July 657 his troops raised pages of the Quran on their lances and Ali accepted arbitration. Some of Ali's soldiers rejected arbitration by men, seceded as the Kharijites, and one of them killed Ali at Kufa in January 661. Mu'awiya took the caliphate and ruled from Damascus; Ali's partisans, the shi'at Ali, became the party from which Shia Islam descends, and the Kharijite view that any pious Muslim could rule was a third answer to the same question.

chapters.title: The Umayyad answer
chapters.s1: A second civil war from 680 to 692 nearly ended the Umayyads, and Caliph Abd al-Malik answered it by giving the state an explicitly Islamic face: the Dome of the Rock, Quranic coinage and an Arabic administration.
chapters.s2: Mu'awiya's designation of his son Yazid in 680 made the caliphate hereditary; Husayn, Ali's son and the Prophet's grandson, rose against it and was killed with most of his small following at Karbala in October 680. Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr then ruled as caliph from Mecca from 683 to 692, and in Kufa al-Mukhtar led a revolt from 685 to 687 in Husayn's name that recruited non-Arab converts, the mawali, on equal terms with Arabs. Abd al-Malik completed the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem in 691-92, with inscriptions addressed to Christians: God has no partner, and the Messiah Jesus was a messenger of God. In 696-97 he replaced Byzantine-style gold coins with dinars bearing only Quranic text, and around 700 Arabic replaced Greek in the Syrian registers, after Persian had given way in Iraq. The inscriptions and coins are among the earliest dated public statements of Islamic doctrine, issued by the state in the middle of a war over who should rule it.

chapters.title: Revolution
chapters.s1: Expansion to Spain and Sindh carried the Arab state to its limits and filled it with converts it still taxed as subjects, and a coalition of converts, settlers and the Prophet's kin overthrew the Umayyads in 750.
chapters.s2: The commander Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed to Spain in 711 and Muhammad ibn al-Qasim took Sindh in 712, but the siege of Constantinople in 717-718 failed and the frontiers stopped moving. Governors short of revenue kept collecting the poll tax from converts and treated Berber Muslims as a conquered people, and the Berbers rose in 740 under Kharijite preachers, destroyed the Arab cavalry of Ifriqiya at the Battle of the Nobles and took the western Maghreb out of the caliphate for good. In Khurasan, Abu Muslim raised the black banners at Merv in June 747 for an unnamed member of the Prophet's family, drawing Arab settlers, Persian converts and Shia partisans who expected a descendant of Ali. The rebels took Kufa in 749 and proclaimed Abu al-Abbas al-Saffah, descended from the Prophet's uncle Abbas, and Caliph Marwan II's army was destroyed at the Zab in January 750. The Abbasids massacred the Umayyad family, invoking Karbala, and then set aside the Alid hopes they had used, which kept Shi'ism a movement of opposition.

stories.today: About two billion people are Muslim, roughly 85 to 90 per cent Sunni and 10 to 15 per cent Shia. Iran's 1979 constitution vests authority in a senior jurist acting for the hidden twelfth imam of Ali's line, and the Ashura commemoration of Karbala is still the central Shia ritual.

arc.title: The Unwinnable War
arc.sub: Mediterranean powers against Iranian empires, 550 BCE to 651 CE
arc.thesis: For eleven centuries the Mediterranean powers and the Iranian empires could defeat, raid and humiliate each other but could not hold each other's heartlands, and the one sustained attempt to end the contest by conquest, Khosrow II's war of 602-628, exhausted both so far that the Arabs took all of Iran and Rome's richest provinces within a generation.
assumptions: Assumes distance and terrain, the Zagros, the Syrian steppe and the Armenian highlands, set the limit of conquest more than ideology or leadership did.

Assumes three Iranian dynasties, and the Macedonian kingdom that ruled Iran between them, can be read as one side of one contest; the participants read it so, from Ardashir I's reported claim to the Achaemenid lands to Heraclius's recovery of the True Cross.
Assumes the Arab conquest of Iran owed more to Persian exhaustion than to Arab strength; the atlas grades the two together.
arc.disconfirm: If the thesis were wrong, a conquest of the other side's core should have held for generations without breaking the conqueror. Rome's three captures of Ctesiphon (116, 165, 197) and Khosrow II's decade in Syria and Egypt fit the thesis; Alexander's conquest of Iran is the test case against it.
arc.awkward: Alexander III of Macedon took the entire Achaemenid empire in four campaigning seasons, 334-330 BCE, and his Seleucid successors ruled the Iranian plateau for about 160 years. The stalemate holds from about 300 BCE, once the Macedonian kingdoms faced each other and Rome; it fails for the one case in which the Iranian side had a single king whose defeat and death delivered the whole system.

stories.title: The Delegated Empire
stories.sub: Achaemenid Persia and the Greeks, 522 to 330 BCE
stories.thesis: Achaemenid Persia ruled through satraps, local elites and fixed tribute, which made it cheap to run and able to absorb its Greek defeats and buy back its position with silver, and the same delegation let Alexander capture the whole system by destroying one king and seizing his treasuries.
assumptions: Assumes the defeats of 480-479 were peripheral to Persian power; the Aegean coast's tribute was small against the revenues of Babylonia and Egypt.
Assumes the Greek narrative sources overstate Persian decline; the Persepolis tablets and Babylonian archives show an administration working to the end.
Assumes Alexander's speed owed more to the Persian system than to Macedonian tactics.
stories.disconfirm: If the thesis were wrong, Persian revenue, territory or cohesion should show steady decline from 479. Egypt's sixty years of independence from 404 is the strongest case for that reading; its reconquest in 343 is the strongest case against.
stories.awkward: Court murders killed Xerxes I in 465, Artaxerxes III in 338 and his son Arses in 336, and the dynasty's succession crises gave both Cyrus the Younger and Alexander their openings. The delegated system ran well; the dynasty at its top was its weakest part.

chapters.title: The system
chapters.s1: Darius I turned Cyrus's conquests into a system of satrapies, fixed tribute and royal roads that could absorb defeats at its edges, and it outlived him by 156 years.
chapters.s2: Persian King Darius I took the throne in 522 by killing Gaumata, the man he called an impostor posing as Cyrus's son, and spent his first year putting down revolts in nearly every province; the Behistun inscription, in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, is his account of that year. He then fixed the empire in some 20 satrapies paying assessed tribute in silver, linked Susa to Sardis by a road of about 2,500 km with relay stations, and began Persepolis around 518. Local elites, temples and laws stayed in place under Persian governors, which kept the cost of rule low. Thousands of Elamite tablets from Persepolis, covering about 509 to 493, record rations of grain and wine issued to workers by the jar. The Scythian campaign of about 513 failed against the nomads but left Thrace and the kingdom of Macedon under Persian authority, so Alexander's ancestors began as Persian vassals.

chapters.title: The western overreach
chapters.s1: The system's reach to the Aegean drew Persia into a war with mainland Greece that it lost at sea and on land without losing anything that carried its revenue.
chapters.s2: The Greek cities of Ionia revolted in 499 against the tyrants Persia ruled them through; Athens and Eretria sent ships and burned Sardis in 498, and Darius needed six years and the naval victory at Lade in 494 to end it. The expedition that landed at Marathon in 490 under the commanders Datis and Artaphernes was a punitive raid with a political aim, to restore the exiled Athenian tyrant Hippias, who sailed with it. Xerxes I had to suppress a revolt in Egypt and two in Babylon before he could invade in 480, and Babylon lost its standing as a privileged city afterwards. Salamis in 480 and Plataea and Mycale in 479 ended Persian designs on mainland Greece and cost the Aegean coast. The core provinces stayed intact, and Xerxes ruled them until courtiers murdered him in 465.

chapters.title: Silver over spears
chapters.s1: Persia recovered with money what it had lost with armies, and in 387 the Great King dictated the terms of peace among the Greek cities.
chapters.s2: From 412 the satraps Tissaphernes at Sardis and Pharnabazus at Dascylium paid for Sparta's fleet against Athens in return for recognition of the King's claim to the Ionian cities, and the subsidies of Cyrus the Younger from 407 financed the fleet that won the Peloponnesian War at Aegospotami in 405. Egypt broke away in 404 and stayed independent for sixty years, the empire's largest loss. Cyrus the Younger marched on his brother Artaxerxes II in 401 with about 10,000 Greek mercenaries and died at Cunaxa; the mercenaries' retreat to the Black Sea taught Greeks that a Persian heartland could be crossed. The King's Peace of 387, read out to Greek envoys at Sardis from a royal rescript, gave Persia the Asian Greek cities and Cyprus and made the King guarantor of autonomy for the rest. Artaxerxes III retook Egypt in 343, and the empire Alexander invaded was larger than at any time since 404.

chapters.title: Captured whole
chapters.s1: The delegation that made Persia cheap to rule let Alexander take it whole: after Gaugamela the satrapies, treasuries and roads passed to the new king with many of their officials in place.
chapters.s2: The court eunuch Bagoas poisoned Artaxerxes III in 338 and his son Arses in 336, and Darius III came to the throne in the year Philip II of Macedon's advance force crossed into Asia. Alexander III of Macedon won at the Granicus in 334, at Issus in 333 and at Gaugamela on 1 October 331, after which Babylon and Susa opened their gates; the treasuries of Susa, Persepolis and Ecbatana yielded on the order of 180,000 talents of silver. Persepolis burned in early 330, and that summer Bessus, satrap of Bactria, murdered Darius III as Alexander closed in. Alexander kept Persian satraps in several provinces, including Mazaeus at Babylon, and adopted Persian court ceremony; his hardest fighting came afterwards, in Bactria and Sogdiana, where local lords had held power under the Achaemenids as well. His death in 323 left the empire to his generals, and Iran became the eastern half of a Macedonian kingdom run from Babylon and Syria.

stories.today: Persepolis (inscribed 1979), Pasargadae (2004) and Behistun (2006) are UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Iran, and the Behistun text was the key to deciphering Babylonian cuneiform in the 1840s and 1850s. The Cyrus Cylinder, excavated at Babylon in 1879 and held by the British Museum, is used by the Islamic Republic and by Iranian monarchists alike as a symbol of Iranian statehood.

stories.title: The Euphrates Line
stories.sub: Seleucids, Parthians and Rome, 312 BCE to 224 CE
stories.thesis: From Seleucus I to Septimius Severus no power could hold both the Mediterranean coast and the Iranian plateau: the Seleucids lost Iran once Rome pressed them in the west, Rome took Ctesiphon three times and kept none of it, Parthia overran Syria and kept none of it, and the frontier settled on the Euphrates with Armenia as the compromise; Arsacid Parthia fell to a revolt inside Iran that Roman sacks had made possible.
assumptions: Assumes the Seleucid loss of Iran and Rome's failure to take it are the same problem: the distance between the Mediterranean and the plateau.
Assumes Parthia's structure, vassal kings and great noble houses under an Arsacid king, made it hard to conquer and slow to mobilise, and that the same feature kept it from holding Syria.
Assumes the Sasanian revolt of 224 owed something to Roman pressure; it may have been a purely Iranian dynastic event.
stories.disconfirm: If the thesis were wrong, a Roman hold on Babylonia or a Parthian hold on Syria should have lasted beyond a few years. Trajan's provinces lasted from 116 to 117 and the Parthian occupation of Syria from 40 to 38 BCE, so the test is the record of every later attempt.
stories.awkward: Rome did hold part of the far side: Septimius Severus's province of Mesopotamia, with its capital at Nisibis, lasted from about 198 to 363. The stalemate held between the two heartlands; the borderland between them changed hands, and once it moved east it stayed there for 165 years.

chapters.title: The Macedonian inheritance
chapters.s1: Seleucus I rebuilt Alexander's Asian empire from Babylon, and his dynasty spent the next century finding that it could not hold the Iranian plateau and the Mediterranean coast at once.
chapters.s2: Seleucus, a Macedonian cavalry officer who had been satrap of Babylon, retook the city with a small force in 311, and his dynasty counted its years from 312/311 in a continuous era that Syriac Christians still used a thousand years later. He took the eastern satrapies to the Indus, then around 305 ceded the Indian provinces to Chandragupta Maurya for 500 war elephants, which helped him win at Ipsus in 301 and gain north Syria, where he founded Antioch. The dynasty's centre of gravity moved west to Syria and its wars with Ptolemaic Egypt, and the east slipped away: Bactria's governor Diodotus broke off around 250, and the Parni nomads under Arsaces took the province of Parthia between about 247 and 238. Antiochus III marched east from about 210 to 205, besieged Bactra for two years and won recognitions of overlordship from both Parthia and Bactria, which lasted as long as his army stayed.

chapters.title: Rome closes the west
chapters.s1: Rome's defeat of Antiochus III at Magnesia in 190 cut the Seleucids off from Anatolia and its revenues and began a decline that Parthia completed from the east.
chapters.s2: Antiochus III crossed into Greece in 192 and was beaten at Thermopylae in 191 and at Magnesia in 190 by a Roman army under Lucius Cornelius Scipio, with his brother Scipio Africanus attached as legate. The Treaty of Apamea in 188 pushed the Seleucid frontier back to the Taurus, imposed an indemnity of 15,000 talents, most of it in twelve annual instalments, and limited the king's fleet and war elephants. Antiochus III died in 187 plundering a temple in Elymais for money. In 168 the Roman envoy Gaius Popillius Laenas drew a circle in the sand around Antiochus IV outside Alexandria and demanded an answer before he stepped out of it; Antiochus gave up Egypt. His attempt to impose Greek cult on Jerusalem soon after provoked the Maccabean revolt, which tied down Seleucid armies in the years Parthia moved west.

chapters.title: Parthia takes the plateau
chapters.s1: Mithridates I took Media and Babylonia from the weakened Seleucids between about 148 and 141, and power over Iran returned to the Tigris under an Iranian dynasty.
chapters.s2: Mithridates I of Parthia took Ecbatana around 148 and was minting coins at Seleucia on the Tigris, the largest Greek city in Asia, by 141. The Seleucid counter-offensive under Demetrius II ended with his capture in 139; he spent ten years as an honoured prisoner married to a Parthian princess. Antiochus VII Sidetes, the last Seleucid king with a full field army, retook Babylonia in 130 and was killed in Media in 129, and Phraates II's victory ended Seleucid claims east of the Euphrates. The Arsacids kept the Greek cities and their councils, used Greek on their coins and ruled through vassal kings and great noble houses, which made the state hard to destroy and slow to mobilise. Ctesiphon, across the Tigris from Seleucia, became the Arsacid royal city and stayed the seat of Iranian kings until 637.

chapters.title: Carrhae
chapters.s1: The Seleucid collapse left Rome and Parthia face to face on the Euphrates, and Carrhae in 53 BCE showed that Parthian horse archers supplied by a camel train could destroy a Roman army in Mesopotamia.
chapters.s2: The first official contact came in about 96, when the Roman governor Lucius Cornelius Sulla met the Parthian envoy Orobazus on the Euphrates and took the centre seat; Mithridates II had the envoy executed for allowing it. Pompey's settlement of 64 ended the Seleucid kingdom and made Syria a Roman province bordering Parthia. Marcus Licinius Crassus invaded in 53 without a pretext, and the Parthian general Surena, with about 9,000 horse archers, 1,000 armoured cavalry and 1,000 camels carrying spare arrows, destroyed his seven legions at Carrhae; some 20,000 Romans died and 10,000 were taken prisoner. Crassus's death removed the third partner from the arrangement between Caesar and Pompey and hastened the civil war of 49. A Parthian army under the prince Pacorus and the Roman renegade Quintus Labienus overran Syria in 40 and was expelled by 38, and Mark Antony's invasion of Media Atropatene in 36 lost about 24,000 men in the retreat.

chapters.title: The Armenian compromise
chapters.s1: Armenia, the one territory both empires needed and neither could hold, became the frontier's safety valve when Rome and Parthia agreed in 63 CE that an Arsacid would rule it under Roman investiture.
chapters.s2: Armenia's highlands flank both the upper Euphrates and the road into Media, so whichever power held it threatened the other's interior. The Roman Emperor Augustus recovered Crassus's standards by negotiation in 20 BCE and paired the deal with a Roman-installed king in Armenia, and for eighty years the two empires fought through rival candidates for its throne. The general Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo took the Armenian capital Artaxata in 58, but a second Roman army surrendered at Rhandeia in 62, and the treaty agreed there in 63 split the difference: Tiridates, brother of the Parthian King Vologases I, would be king, crowned by Nero. Tiridates travelled overland to Rome in 66 with some 3,000 horsemen, and Nero placed the diadem on his head in the Forum. The formula of an Arsacid king approved by Rome kept the peace for about fifty years, until Trajan annexed Armenia in 114, and Arsacids held the Armenian throne until 428.

chapters.title: Sacked from the west
chapters.s1: Rome sacked Ctesiphon three times in eighty years and kept only northern Mesopotamia, while the repeated humiliations drained the Arsacid dynasty's standing with its own nobles.
chapters.s2: Trajan annexed Armenia in 114, took Ctesiphon in 116 and reached the Persian Gulf, but revolts in the conquered cities and among the Jews of the eastern diaspora forced him back, and Hadrian gave up Armenia and Mesopotamia on his accession in 117. Avidius Cassius burned Seleucia and Ctesiphon in 165, and Seleucia, which had held perhaps several hundred thousand people, never recovered; the returning legions brought back the epidemic known as the Antonine Plague. Septimius Severus sacked Ctesiphon in 197 and created the province of Mesopotamia with its capital at Nisibis, the one Roman gain beyond the Euphrates that lasted. The last Parthian king, Artabanus IV, beat the Emperor Macrinus near Nisibis in 217 and forced him to pay 200 million sesterces. Seven years later Ardashir, a sub-king in Persis, killed Artabanus in battle and ended the dynasty.

stories.today: The Euphrates crossings at Zeugma and Samosata, the main Roman bridgeheads toward Parthia, now lie partly or wholly under the reservoirs of Turkey's Birecik and Atatürk dams. The site of Seleucia and Ctesiphon lies about 35 km south-east of Baghdad, and the dating era Seleucus founded in 312/311 BCE survived in Syriac church use into modern times.

stories.title: Mutual Exhaustion
stories.sub: Sasanian Iran and Rome, 224 to 651
stories.thesis: Sasanian Iran was a more centralised and more ideological rival than Parthia, and after a century of Persian victories the two empires settled into a managed rivalry of fortresses, subsidies, treaties and Arab client kings; Khosrow II's attempt to break it by conquest from 602 exhausted both, and his abolition of the Lakhmid kingdom opened the desert frontier the Arab armies crossed in 633.
assumptions: Assumes the managed rivalry of the fifth and sixth centuries was a working equilibrium, which the wars of 502-506, 527-532, 540-562 and 572-591 make questionable.
Assumes the Arab conquest of Iran owed more to the war of 602-628 and the civil war of 628-632 than to Arab numbers or doctrine.
Assumes the Lakhmid kingdom served Persia as a buffer; it also served as a raiding arm against Roman Syria, and its removal may have had other motives.
stories.disconfirm: If the thesis were wrong, a Sasanian state that had not fought the war of 602-628 should still have lost Iraq to the Arabs on a similar timescale. The speed of the conquest of Iraq, from Khalid ibn al-Walid's raids in 633 to the fall of Ctesiphon in 637, would then measure Arab strength more than Persian weakness.
stories.awkward: Rome fought the same war, won it, and still lost Syria, Palestine and Egypt to the same Arab armies within fifteen years of Heraclius's victory. Exhaustion explains why both empires lost their southern provinces; it leaves open why Rome survived in Anatolia while the Sasanian state vanished entirely, and the answer may lie in Constantinople's walls and the lack of any Iranian equivalent once Ctesiphon fell.

chapters.title: A sharper rival
chapters.s1: Ardashir I replaced the Parthians in 224 with a dynasty from Persis that centralised Iran, bound kingship to the Zoroastrian priesthood and attacked Roman Mesopotamia within six years.
chapters.s2: Ardashir, a sub-king in Persis, killed Artabanus IV at Hormozdgan on 28 April 224 and was crowned at Ctesiphon. The new dynasty replaced most Parthian vassal kings with princes of its own house, founded cities under royal names and tied the throne to the Zoroastrian priesthood, while great Parthian houses such as the Suren and the Karen kept their lands and commands inside the new order. Ardashir invaded Roman Mesopotamia in 230; Roman writers record his claim to all the lands the Achaemenids had ruled, a claim the Persian sources never state. The Emperor Severus Alexander's counter-offensive of 232 was costly for both sides. The fall in 241 of Hatra, the desert city that had become a Roman ally, opened the road to the Euphrates and added an eastern front to the military crisis that broke the Roman imperial succession after 235.

chapters.title: Shapur's victories
chapters.s1: Shapur I killed, bought off and captured Roman emperors in sixteen years, the worst Roman humiliation in the East, and annexed nothing west of the Euphrates.
chapters.s2: Gordian III died after the battle of Misiche in 244, and his successor Philip the Arab paid 500,000 denarii to bring the army home. Shapur I destroyed a Roman army of some 60,000 at Barbalissos around 253 and plundered Antioch, and in 260 captured the Emperor Valerian at Edessa with his praetorian prefect and senators. Roman prisoners were settled in Khuzestan and Persis, where tradition credits them with building Gundishapur and the bridge-dam at Shushtar. Shapur's inscription on the Ka'ba-ye Zartosht at Naqsh-e Rostam, in Middle Persian, Parthian and Greek, claims 36 Roman cities taken in the campaign of 253 alone. Odaenathus, the ruler of Palmyra, harried the Persian army on its way home, and Shapur's gains of 253-260 came down to plunder and skilled labour; the Euphrates line held.

chapters.title: Armenia divided
chapters.s1: Christianity turned the contest over Armenia into a religious one, and the two empires settled it around 387 by dividing the kingdom, Persia taking about four-fifths.
chapters.s2: The Roman Caesar Galerius's victory over Narseh in 298 brought the Peace of Nisibis of 299, which gave Rome five districts beyond the Tigris and the right to invest Armenia's kings. Armenia's King Tiridates III adopted Christianity in the early fourth century, by tradition in 301, and Constantine's conversion made Armenian Christians a Roman interest inside a Persian sphere. Shapur II spent decades recovering the losses of 299; Julian's invasion of 363 reached Ctesiphon and ended with his death, and his successor Jovian gave up Nisibis, Singara and the districts beyond the Tigris to save the army. After the partition the Persians abolished the Arsacid monarchy in their share of Armenia in 428. Yazdegerd I let the Christians of his empire organise as a single church at the Synod of Seleucia-Ctesiphon in 410, which made them a Persian institution rather than a Roman fifth column. Yazdegerd II's attempt to impose Zoroastrianism on Armenia produced the revolt crushed at Avarayr in 451, and by 484 Persia had conceded the Armenians their faith.

chapters.title: Managed rivalry
chapters.s1: After the partition the two empires ran their rivalry through fortress lines, Roman payments and Arab client kings, and Khosrow I and Justinian I bought time from each other with treaties neither expected to last.
chapters.s2: Kavad I's war of 502-506, fought partly to extract Roman money for his debts to the Hephthalites, led the Emperor Anastasius I to build the fortress of Dara 18 km from Persian Nisibis. Justinian I made the Ghassanid chief al-Harith ibn Jabala supreme phylarch of Rome's Arab allies in 529 to match the Lakhmid kings of al-Hira, Persia's clients since the late third century. Khosrow I, who came to the throne in 531 after the massacre of the Mazdakite sect and went on to reform the land tax, signed the Eternal Peace in 532 for a payment of 11,000 pounds of gold, and Justinian used the quiet to send Belisarius against Vandal Africa in 533. Khosrow broke the peace in 540 while Justinian's armies were in Italy, sacked Antioch and resettled its people in a new city near Ctesiphon he named Weh Antiok Khosrow, 'Khosrow's better Antioch'. The Fifty-Year Peace of 562 fixed Roman payments of 30,000 gold coins a year and channelled trade through named customs posts, and it lasted ten years.

chapters.title: Khosrow II's gamble
chapters.s1: Khosrow II used the murder of his patron Maurice in 602 to launch a war for the whole Roman East, held Syria, Palestine and Egypt for more than a decade, and lost it all when Heraclius struck at Iran's undefended north.
chapters.s2: Sasanian King Khosrow II owed his throne to the Roman Emperor Maurice, whose army restored him at Blarathon in 591 in exchange for most of Persian Armenia and Iberia. When the centurion Phocas murdered Maurice in 602, Khosrow declared war as his avenger, and in the same year deposed the Lakhmid king al-Nu'man III and replaced the dynasty with a governor. Persian armies took Dara in 604, held Syria by 613 and took Jerusalem in 614, from where they carried the True Cross to Ctesiphon, and Alexandria in 619; the loss of Egyptian grain ended Constantinople's free bread ration in 618. The Avar and Persian siege of Constantinople in 626 failed because the Roman fleet kept the two armies apart across the Bosporus. The Emperor Heraclius, campaigning through the Caucasus with Western Turkic allies, won at Nineveh in December 627 and sacked the royal palace at Dastagird. Rome paid for the war by melting church plate, and Khosrow by taxes that turned his own nobles against him.

chapters.title: The open desert
chapters.s1: The war and the civil war after it left Sasanian Iraq without its Arab frontier guard, a settled king or a field army, and the Arab armies took the empire's richest province in four years.
chapters.s2: Khosrow II was deposed and killed in February 628 in a coup that put his son Kavad II on the throne; Kavad made peace and died within months, and some ten rulers, among them Khosrow's daughters Boran and Azarmidokht, claimed the throne in four years. Both empires had already stripped their Arab buffers: Rome arrested the Ghassanid king al-Mundhir in 581 and the federation broke up, and the Bakr tribes' victory over a Persian force at Dhi Qar, sometime between 604 and 611, showed that the Persian desert edge was open once the Lakhmids were gone. Khalid ibn al-Walid's raids of 633 took al-Hira, the old Lakhmid capital. At al-Qadisiyyah, probably in 636, the Arab army under Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas destroyed the imperial army and killed its commander, Rostam Farrokhzad, and Ctesiphon fell in March 637 after a three-month siege. The Sawad, the irrigated plain of lower Iraq, had supplied the largest share of Sasanian revenue, and its loss left the dynasty a kingdom of the mountains.

chapters.title: The flight east
chapters.s1: The plateau held out for fourteen years after Ctesiphon, long enough to show that Iran's provinces could resist on their own and too short to save a dynasty that could no longer pay a central army.
chapters.s2: Yazdegerd III raised a last imperial army, which the Arab commander al-Nu'man ibn Muqarrin destroyed at Nahavand in December 642 at the cost of his own life. After Nahavand the conquest went province by province: cities such as Hamadan, Isfahan and Rey made separate terms, and Istakhr in Persis surrendered, revolted and was sacked in 650-651 with heavy loss of life. Yazdegerd fled east through Kerman and Sistan to Merv, where a miller killed him in 651, by tradition at the instigation of the local governor Mahoe Suri. His son Peroz III appealed to Tang China, which named him governor of a nominal Persian command at Zaranj in 661; he died at the Tang court around 678. The caliphate kept Persian-speaking officials and Sasanian tax registers in Iraq and Iran until the 690s, and Persian, unlike Aramaic and Coptic, survived the conquest to return as a literary language in the ninth and tenth centuries.

stories.today: Saddam Hussein's government called Iraq's 1980-88 war with Iran 'Saddam's Qadisiyyah', reading the battle of 636 as an Arab victory over Persia. The Taq Kasra, the great vault of the Sasanian palace at Ctesiphon and the largest surviving Sasanian building, lost part of its structure in 2019, and emergency stabilisation funded by the international heritage fund ALIPH began in 2021.

arc.title: Who Pays the Legions
arc.sub: the Roman Empire from Augustus to the Arab conquests, 27 BCE to 641 CE
arc.thesis: The Roman Empire was a system for turning Mediterranean taxes into frontier armies, and it survived civil war, plague and a change of religion for as long as that loop held; it broke where the tax base was cut away, in the West when the Vandals took Africa in 439 and in the East when the Arabs took Syria and Egypt between 636 and 641.
assumptions: Assumes the army was the state's largest cost and the emperors' real electorate, which is clear for the first three centuries and less so once the civil bureaucracy grew after Diocletian.
Assumes fiscal capacity can be read from fragmentary evidence: coin fineness, pay scales and the handful of budget figures the sources give.
Assumes the state that survived in Constantinople after 641 was a successor that had to rebuild the loop on a smaller base.
arc.disconfirm: If the thesis were wrong, the West should have fallen while its revenue base was intact, or survived after losing it. The test is 406 to 476: a western government that kept raising and paying field armies at the old scale after 439, or one that collapsed from an internal cause before the provinces went, would break the fiscal reading.
arc.awkward: The worst crisis before 400 came with the tax base largely intact. Between 235 and 284 the empire lost no core revenue province for good and still came closer to breaking than at any time before the fifth century, because its armies made and unmade emperors faster than any treasury could settle them. The loop can fail from the army's end as well as the taxpayers'.

stories.title: The Augustan Bargain
stories.sub: the principate and its army, 31 BCE to 192 CE
stories.thesis: Augustus's settlement held for two centuries because it made the emperor the legions' paymaster and stopped the frontier where the taxes could carry it; each time it was reopened, in 69 and after 165, the army or the frontier had outgrown the money.
assumptions: Assumes the legions' loyalty was bought more than believed, which undervalues the oath, the standards and the imperial cult in the camps.
Assumes the halts at the Rhine in 16 and the Euphrates in 117 were fiscal choices; both also had strategic and personal motives.
stories.disconfirm: If the thesis were wrong, the civil war of 69 should have been settled by the Senate or a dynastic claim. It was settled by which provincial army reached Italy first; a principate in which the Senate chose emperors against the armies and made it stick would refute the reading.
stories.awkward: The longest stable stretch, 96 to 180, came under emperors chosen by adoption rather than by soldiers, and the armies accepted every one of them. Something besides pay held the legions in that century, perhaps only the habit of an orderly succession.

chapters.title: The bargain
chapters.s1: Augustus turned the armies of the civil wars into a standing force paid by the state through himself, and that arrangement was the empire's working constitution whatever forms the Senate kept.
chapters.s2: Octavian came out of Actium in 31 BCE with some sixty legions and no rival; he cut them to twenty-eight and settled the discharged men on land bought largely with Egyptian treasure. In 27 BCE he took as his own command the provinces that held most of the legions, leaving the Senate the unarmed ones. The military treasury of 6 CE, opened with 170 million sesterces of his own money and fed by a 5 per cent tax on citizens' inheritances, moved veterans' pensions from generals' promises to a state fund. Roman citizens had paid no direct tax since 167 BCE, and the Senate fought the levy for years. When Augustus died in 14 CE the Rhine and Pannonian legions mutinied within weeks over pay and length of service.

chapters.title: The limit
chapters.s1: The loss of three legions in Germany in 9 CE fixed the northern frontier at the Rhine, because the empire could not replace them without taxes its citizens would not pay.
chapters.s2: Publius Quinctilius Varus, governor of the new province between Rhine and Elbe, was led into the Teutoburg forest by Arminius, a Cheruscan prince who held Roman citizenship and equestrian rank, and the Seventeenth, Eighteenth and Nineteenth legions died there. Their numbers were never issued again. Augustus had just spent three years putting down the Pannonian revolt and had already enrolled freed slaves to fill the ranks; there was no reserve. Germanicus's campaigns of 14-16 recovered two of the lost eagles, and Tiberius recalled him in 16 with the province unrestored, since Germany had no cities to tax. Britain, invaded by Claudius in 43 for a new emperor's prestige, needed four legions, about an eighth of the army, and on most reckonings never covered their cost.

chapters.title: The secret
chapters.s1: Nero's fall in 68 showed that an emperor could be made by a provincial army, and the civil war of 69 went to whichever legions reached Italy first.
chapters.s2: The Praetorian Guard had already chosen an emperor in 41, when it murdered Caligula and installed Claudius, who paid each guardsman 15,000 sesterces and set the price of later accessions. Nero cut the denarius to 1/96 of a pound of silver in 64 to stretch his revenue after the Great Fire. When the governors of Gaul and Spain turned on him in 68 the Senate followed, and Galba, Otho and Vitellius each fell within the next twelve months. Vespasian, proclaimed at Alexandria on 1 July 69 with the eastern legions and Egypt's grain in hand, won because the Danube legions declared for him and marched first. He paid for the war by raising and in places doubling provincial tribute, and the treasure taken from Jerusalem in 70 helped build the Colosseum.

chapters.title: The dividend
chapters.s1: The second century was the bargain at its most profitable, a fixed frontier, a paid army and a taxable trading economy, and Hadrian chose to hold it rather than enlarge it.
chapters.s2: Emperor Domitian raised legionary pay by a third in the mid-80s, to 300 denarii a year, and the army already took most of what the state spent. Trajan's conquest of Dacia in 106 paid for itself in royal gold and mines; his march to the Persian Gulf in 116 did not, as Mesopotamia revolted behind him and the Jewish diaspora rose in Cyrenaica, Egypt and Cyprus. Hadrian gave up the new eastern provinces in 117 and in 122 began an 80-mile wall across northern Britain. Inside the line, Indian goods landed at the Red Sea ports paid a 25 per cent import duty, and the count of dated Mediterranean shipwrecks and the lead from Roman silver smelting preserved in Greenland ice both reach their ancient peak between the first century BCE and the second century CE. Adoption delivered four successions without civil war between 98 and 161.

chapters.title: The shock
chapters.s1: The epidemic that soldiers carried home from Mesopotamia in 165 struck the empire at its fiscal peak, and two decades of war on the Danube followed while the tax base shrank.
chapters.s2: Co-emperor Lucius Verus's army brought the disease back from the sack of Seleucia on the Tigris; it reached Rome in 166 and recurred into the 180s, and most modern estimates put deaths near a tenth of a population of about 75 million. The Greenland lead record falls sharply in the same decades, as mining and smelting contracted. Marcomanni and Quadi crossed the Danube and besieged Aquileia in 170, the first enemy army in Italy in nearly three centuries. Emperor Marcus Aurelius sold palace treasures at auction in Trajan's Forum to fund the war, enlisted slaves and gladiators, and spent most of his last decade on the Danube. His son Commodus made peace in 180, and his murder on the last day of 192 left no heir and no rule of succession.

stories.today: Hadrian's Wall has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987, and the Lower German Limes and the western Danube Limes were added in 2021 as Frontiers of the Roman Empire. Romanian, a Romance language spoken across the former province, is the main claimed legacy of the 165 years Rome held Dacia; whether its speakers descend from the provincials or from Latin speakers who later crossed the Danube is still disputed.

stories.title: The Soldiers' Throne
stories.sub: from Septimius Severus to Constantine, 193 to 337
stories.thesis: In the third century the armies' claims on the throne and the treasury outran the silver that paid them, and the empire was saved by soldier-emperors from the Danube who built a heavier state that taxed in kind and paid in gold.
assumptions: Assumes debasement was a symptom of fiscal strain; several emperors used it as a deliberate policy that worked for a time.
Assumes the Sasanian revival was the larger new cost; the German and Gothic pressure arrived in the same decades and the two are hard to separate.
Assumes the reforms of Diocletian and Constantine were a solution; the larger and costlier state they built may be one cause of the West's later weakness.
stories.disconfirm: If the thesis were wrong, the usurpations of 235 to 284 should track something other than pay and frontier defeats: dynastic accident, senatorial politics or regional separatism alone. The Gallic and Palmyrene breakaways argue for regionalism; both formed to defend frontiers the centre could not reach, which keeps them inside the thesis, but a breakaway that formed without a military emergency would count against it.
stories.awkward: Military recovery and monetary collapse ran in opposite directions. The steepest price rises in the Egyptian papyri follow Aurelian's restoration of 274 and come again under Diocletian, the emperors who ended the crisis, so restoring the army's loop did not restore the coin.

chapters.title: The pay rise
chapters.s1: Septimius Severus took the throne in 193 with the Danube legions and kept it by paying the army more than the silver supply could carry.
chapters.s2: After the Praetorian Guard killed Emperor Pertinax and sold the throne to the senator Didius Julianus, Septimius Severus, governor of Upper Pannonia, marched on Rome, dismissed the Guard and refilled it from his own Danube legions. Around 197 he raised legionary pay from 300 to 400 denarii, let serving soldiers live with their wives, and added three new legions; to pay for it the denarius fell from about 78 to 54 per cent silver by 196. His son Caracalla raised pay again by half and in 212 made nearly every free inhabitant a citizen, bringing millions under the inheritance tax that funded veterans' pensions, whose rate he doubled to 10 per cent. His antoninianus of 215 passed for two denarii and held the silver of about one and a half. Severus's reported deathbed advice to his sons, to enrich the soldiers and scorn everyone else, is the dynasty's own summary.

chapters.title: Two fronts
chapters.s1: A reformed Persian monarchy in the east and new Germanic and Gothic coalitions in the north arrived together, and the army Severus had bought began killing emperors who could not win on both fronts.
chapters.s2: Ardashir I overthrew the last Parthian king in 224, claimed the lands of the Achaemenids, and took Nisibis and Carrhae from Rome in the late 230s. Emperor Severus Alexander, who tried to buy peace from the Alamanni on the Rhine in 235, was murdered by his own troops near Mainz, and his successor Maximinus, a Thracian officer, never set foot in Rome. At least twenty-six men claimed the throne in the next fifty years, and most died at their soldiers' hands. In 251 the Goths killed Emperor Decius and his son at Abritus in Moesia, the first emperor to die fighting a foreign enemy. An epidemic recorded at Alexandria in 249 reached Rome by 251 and reportedly killed 5,000 a day there at its height, cutting recruits and taxpayers at the same time.

chapters.title: The breaking
chapters.s1: Shapur I's capture of Emperor Valerian in 260 split the empire in three, as frontier armies that the centre could not protect made emperors of their own.
chapters.s2: Shah Shapur I had destroyed a Roman army at Barbalissos and sacked Antioch in the 250s; at Edessa in 260 he took Valerian prisoner, the first Roman emperor captured by a foreign enemy, and his rock reliefs at Naqsh-e Rostam and Bishapur still show Roman emperors submitting to him. Valerian's son Gallienus kept Italy, Africa and the Danube. On the Rhine the general Postumus was proclaimed by his troops after a quarrel over booty, and his Gallic Empire held Gaul, Britain and for a time Spain until 274. In the east Odaenathus of Palmyra drove Shapur back under a Roman title, and in 270 his widow Zenobia took Egypt and its grain. By then the antoninianus was a bronze coin with a silver wash, and the mints of Gaul and Italy were striking against each other.

chapters.title: The restoration
chapters.s1: Aurelian, a Danubian officer, reunited the three parts between 272 and 274 and paid for it by giving up Dacia and walling Rome.
chapters.s2: Proclaimed by the legions at Sirmium in 270, Aurelian drove Alamanni and Juthungi out of Italy and in 271 began a brick wall 19 kilometres round the capital, Rome's first new circuit since the fourth century BCE. He withdrew the army and administration from Dacia, the province Trajan had taken for its gold, and resettled them south of the Danube. He took Palmyra in 272 and razed it after a second revolt in 273, and the Gallic emperor Tetricus surrendered at Châlons in 274. His coin reform of about 274 retariffed the antoninianus at a stated 5 per cent silver, and prices in Egypt rose several-fold within a few years. His own officers murdered him in Thrace in 275.

chapters.title: The rebuild
chapters.s1: Diocletian rebuilt the bargain on a new base: more emperors to stop usurpers, a larger army, and a tax assessed in kind on land and labour that no longer depended on the coin.
chapters.s2: Diocletian, another Danubian officer, was acclaimed by the army at Nicomedia in 284 and ruled for twenty-one years, the longest reign since Antoninus Pius. From 1 March 293 four rulers, two senior Augusti and two Caesars, each had an army and a court, so that no frontier lay far from an emperor who could stop a local usurper. The army grew to perhaps 400,000 or more, the provinces were cut into about a hundred under twelve dioceses, and from at least 297 the state assessed land and labour in fixed units and collected much of the tax as grain, meat and cloth for the troops. The price edict of 301 fixed maximum prices for more than a thousand goods and services on pain of death and was dead within a few years; a currency edict the same year doubled the face value of the coinage.

chapters.title: The new centre
chapters.s1: Constantine broke the tetrarchy he inherited and kept its fiscal machine, adding a gold coin that held its value for seven centuries and a capital at the junction of the frontiers that mattered.
chapters.s2: The army at York proclaimed Constantine on his father's death in July 306 in breach of the tetrarchic rules, and eighteen years of war among the successors ended at Chrysopolis in 324, where he defeated Licinius and became sole emperor. His solidus, struck at 72 to the pound of gold from about 309, became the coin in which the state paid salaries and demanded taxes; gold taken from temple treasuries after 324 helped supply it, while the silver and bronze coins kept losing value beneath it. He dedicated Constantinople on 11 May 330 on the strait between the Danube and Euphrates fronts, gave it a Senate, and from 332 fed it with a free grain ration shipped from Egypt. The eastern half of the empire, with the richer cities and the larger tax base, now had its own centre.

stories.today: The solidus lives on in the 's' of the old British pounds, shillings and pence, in the Italian 'soldo' and, through the French 'solde' for pay, in the word 'soldier'. Istanbul, the city dedicated in 330, had about 15.7 million people at the end of 2024.

stories.title: The Western Collapse
stories.sub: from Adrianople to the Ostrogothic kingdom, 376 to 493
stories.thesis: The western empire fell because armed peoples settled inside it carved away its tax base province by province faster than it could raise armies to recover them, and the loss of Africa in 439 was the point after which recovery was out of reach.
assumptions: Assumes outside pressure mattered more than internal decay; a long tradition holds that the West had hollowed out before 376.
Assumes the East could not have saved the West; it tried in 468 and failed, but one failure is a thin sample.
Assumes 476 marks something real; in Italy the Senate, the law and the tax collectors carried on under Odoacer and Theodoric.
stories.disconfirm: If the thesis were wrong, the western government should have been bankrupt before the provinces went, or should have kept paying field armies after 439. The laws of 444, in which Valentinian III's government admitted it could not feed new recruits, come five years after Carthage fell; a comparable admission from before 406 would weaken the claim.
stories.awkward: The East faced the same Goths and Huns, lost the larger army at Adrianople, paid Attila thousands of pounds of gold, and survived intact. Geography did much of the work: the Theodosian Walls and the Bosporus kept invaders out of Anatolia, Syria and Egypt, where the East's taxes came from, and nothing comparable stood in front of Gaul, Spain or Africa.

chapters.title: The breach
chapters.s1: The defeat at Adrianople in 378 put an armed Gothic people permanently inside the empire, on terms that let it keep its own leaders and its own army.
chapters.s2: Tervingi and Greuthungi Goths, pushed by the Huns north of the Black Sea, were admitted across the Danube in 376 as recruits and settlers, and Roman officers' profiteering on their food supply drove them to revolt. Emperor Valens attacked them at Adrianople on 9 August 378 without waiting for his nephew Gratian's western army, and about two-thirds of the eastern field army died with him. Theodosius I could not rebuild fast enough to expel the Goths, and the treaty of 3 October 382 settled them on the lower Danube as a federated people under their own chiefs, owing soldiers rather than taxes. Every later settlement in the West followed that precedent: an armed group that served Rome for pay or land and could withhold its service to raise the price.

chapters.title: The division
chapters.s1: Theodosius's death in 395 left the empire to two boy emperors whose courts treated each other as rivals, and the Gothic army in the Balkans learned to sell its service to each in turn.
chapters.s2: Theodosius I beat the western usurper Eugenius at the Frigidus in September 394 with Gothic federates in the front line, where they took the heaviest losses, and died at Milan in January 395. His sons Arcadius, 17 or 18, in Constantinople and Honorius, 10, in the West were run by regents, the half-Vandal general Stilicho in the West and the prefect Rufinus in the East, who disputed control of the Balkan provinces of Illyricum. Alaric, leading the Balkan Goths from 395, extracted commands and pay from each court in turn. The East used the respite to build: the land walls of Constantinople, begun around 404 and finished by 413, held against every assault until 1453 and kept the East's tax base in Anatolia, Syria and Egypt behind them.

chapters.title: The unravelling
chapters.s1: The crossing of the Rhine at the end of 406 began the dismemberment of the western tax base, and within twelve years Britain was gone, Spain overrun and Rome sacked.
chapters.s2: Vandals, Alans and Suebi crossed the Rhine near Mainz on 31 December 406, while Stilicho's army was in Italy after defeating the Gothic invasion of Radagaisus. Britain's garrison raised its own emperor, Constantine III, who took the remaining troops to Gaul in 407; the island never returned, and in 410 Emperor Honorius told its cities to see to their own defence. Stilicho was executed in August 408, Roman troops then killed the families of federate soldiers across Italy, and perhaps 30,000 of those men joined Alaric. Alaric's Goths sacked Rome on 24 August 410 after Honorius, safe in Ravenna, refused them land and pay. In 418 the government settled the Goths in Aquitaine to fight the invaders in Spain, buying an army with a province whose taxes it would no longer fully collect.

chapters.title: The revenue
chapters.s1: The Vandal capture of Carthage in 439 took the West's richest surviving province, and after it the western government could not pay for the army it needed.
chapters.s2: By the 430s the general Flavius Aetius had steadied Gaul with Hunnic auxiliaries, and Africa, which supplied Rome's grain and a large share of western revenue, was still intact. King Gaiseric took some 80,000 Vandals and Alans across from Spain in 429, besieged Hippo Regius, where its bishop Augustine died in 430, and seized Carthage with its harbour and shipping on 19 October 439. A treaty of 442 accepted the loss. In 444 Emperor Valentinian III's laws conceded that revenue could not feed new recruits or clothe the existing army, added a sales tax of one twenty-fourth, and ended the officials' exemption from the recruit levy. A Vandal fleet now sat astride the sea lanes to Sicily and Italy.

chapters.title: The Huns
chapters.s1: Attila's empire drained the East's gold and pinned the West's army in Gaul when it was needed for Africa, and its sudden end in 453 released the peoples it had held.
chapters.s2: From the 440s Attila ran a confederation from the Hungarian plain that took tribute in gold from Constantinople; after he destroyed an eastern army on the Utus in 447, the peace of 448 raised the annual payment to 2,100 pounds. In 451 he turned west, and Aetius stopped him on the Catalaunian Plains in Champagne with an army whose core was Visigothic. Attila invaded Italy in 452 and withdrew with disease in his army, and he died in 453. His sons lost the subject Germanic peoples at the Nedao in 454, the year Valentinian III killed Aetius with his own hand in the palace. Valentinian was murdered in March 455, and that June a Vandal fleet from Carthage plundered Rome for two weeks.

chapters.title: The last throw
chapters.s1: The joint expedition against Carthage in 468 was the last attempt to recover the West's revenue, and its failure left the western throne a prize for generals until one of them stopped filling it in 476.
chapters.s2: Eastern Emperor Leo I sent more than a thousand ships under his brother-in-law Basiliscus, at a cost that ancient writers put at about 64,000 pounds of gold and 700,000 of silver, and Gaiseric's fire-ships wrecked the fleet off Cape Bon. Without Africa the western emperors were creatures of their generals, and the general Ricimer made or broke five of them between 456 and 472. In 476 the army in Italy demanded land, the general Odoacer gave it to them, deposed the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus, and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople. The Roman tax system carried on in Italy under Odoacer and then under the Ostrogothic king Theodoric, whom Emperor Zeno sent west and who killed Odoacer at a banquet in Ravenna in 493.

stories.today: The kingdoms that replaced the western empire are the ancestors of France, named after Clovis's Franks, and England, named after the Angles. Italy was not again governed from Rome as a single state until 1871.

stories.title: The Spent Surplus
stories.sub: the eastern empire from Anastasius to the Arab conquests, 491 to 641
stories.thesis: The eastern empire spent its sixth-century surplus reconquering the West, lost a large share of its taxpayers to plague, and then fought Persia to mutual exhaustion, so that the Arab armies of the 630s found the provinces that paid for the Roman army held by forces the state could no longer pay.
assumptions: Assumes Justinian's wars drained the East, although the reconquest of Africa probably repaid its cost in tax.
Assumes the plague's mortality was severe and lasting; recent work on papyri, coin finds and pollen argues for a smaller demographic effect.
Assumes Arab success owed much to Roman and Persian exhaustion; the conquerors' cohesion and command would have counted against stronger opponents too.
stories.disconfirm: If the thesis were wrong, Rome should have lost Syria and Egypt with a full treasury and a paid, rested army. Heraclius halved officials' salaries and melted church plate to fund the Persian war; if the army that broke at the Yarmuk had been well funded and at full strength, the cause lies with the conquerors rather than with Roman exhaustion.
stories.awkward: Rome won the war that is supposed to have exhausted it. Heraclius destroyed the Persian army at Nineveh in 627 and recovered every lost province by 630, while Persia fell into civil war and was conquered outright. Exhaustion explains why both lost provinces; Constantinople's walls and the distance of Anatolia explain why one of them survived.

chapters.title: The surplus
chapters.s1: Justinian inherited the largest reserve in the empire's history and spent it recovering Africa and Italy, buying peace from Persia to free the army.
chapters.s2: Emperor Anastasius I restored a sound bronze coinage in 498, converted much tax in kind into gold payments, and left 320,000 pounds of gold at his death in 518. Justinian I, emperor from 527, bought the Perpetual Peace of 532 from Khosrow I of Persia for 11,000 pounds of gold. The Nika riot of January 532, aimed at his tax ministers, nearly drove him from the city, and his general Belisarius ended it by killing some 30,000 people in the Hippodrome. In 533 Belisarius took Vandal Africa with about 15,000 men in a single campaign, and in 535 began the war for Italy, where the Ostrogothic kings still collected Roman taxes through Roman officials. Africa repaid its conquest; Italy took twenty years.

chapters.title: The plague
chapters.s1: Bubonic plague reached the empire in 541, a year after Persia broke the peace, and struck the taxpayers and recruits that a two-front war required.
chapters.s2: Khosrow I invaded Syria in 540 while the army was in Italy, sacked Antioch, and deported its people to a new city he built near Ctesiphon. The plague appeared at Pelusium in Egypt in 541 and reached Constantinople in spring 542, where one eyewitness put deaths at up to 10,000 a day; DNA from sixth-century graves in Bavaria has since confirmed Yersinia pestis as the agent. In 544 Justinian legislated against the higher wages and prices that the labour shortage had produced. The Italian war, close to won in 540, dragged on until 554, when the Pragmatic Sanction restored the landowners of an Italy wrecked by two decades of campaigning.

chapters.title: The mutiny
chapters.s1: Holding Italy, the Danube and the east at once with a plague-thinned treasury pushed Emperor Maurice to economise on the army, and the army's revolt in 602 gave Persia the pretext for the last great war.
chapters.s2: The Lombards entered Italy in 568, three years after Justinian's death, and within a decade held most of the interior. The Avars, steppe horsemen who had taken the Huns' place on the Hungarian plain, took Sirmium in 582 after a two-year siege and opened the Balkans to Slav settlement. Maurice restored the deposed Khosrow II to the Persian throne in 591, gaining much of Armenia, and used the eastern peace to fight on the Danube. He had cut army pay by a quarter in 588, provoking a mutiny in the east, and in 602 he ordered the Balkan army to winter north of the river in Slav country, sparing the treasury the cost of winter quarters. The army marched on Constantinople under the junior officer Phocas and killed Maurice and his sons, and Khosrow invaded in 603 claiming to avenge his patron.

chapters.title: The near-death
chapters.s1: The Persian conquest of Syria, Palestine and Egypt between 611 and 619 took away the provinces that fed and paid the empire, and in 626 Constantinople itself was under siege.
chapters.s2: Heraclius, son of the exarch of Africa, sailed from Carthage and overthrew Phocas in October 610, then lost a battle outside Antioch in 613 that cut the empire's land route to the south. Jerusalem fell in 614 after a three-week siege, and the relic of the True Cross went to Ctesiphon. Shahrbaraz's army entered Egypt in 618 and took Alexandria in June 619; Constantinople's free bread ration, fed by Egyptian grain since 332, was abolished in 618. Heraclius considered moving the capital to Carthage, melted church plate into coin and cut salaries. In summer 626 an Avar and Slav army besieged the city from the European side while a Persian army waited across the Bosporus at Chalcedon, and the Roman fleet kept them apart until the siege failed.

chapters.title: The victory
chapters.s1: Heraclius won the war by marching around the Persian armies into Mesopotamia, and by 630 Rome had its provinces back and Persia was in civil war.
chapters.s2: From 624 Heraclius campaigned through Armenia and Azerbaijan, won an alliance with the Western Turkic khagan Tong Yabghu, whose horsemen joined him at the siege of Tiflis in 627, and late that year marched south into the Sasanian heartland. On 12 December 627 he destroyed the last Persian field army near the ruins of Nineveh. Khosrow II was overthrown and killed by his own nobles in 628, his son Kavad II made peace and died within months, and Persia went through a run of short-lived rulers until Yazdegerd III in 632. Heraclius returned the True Cross to Jerusalem in 629 or 630. The provinces he recovered had been under Persian rule for up to fifteen years, and their garrisons and tax registers had to be rebuilt by a treasury emptied by the war.

chapters.title: The collapse
chapters.s1: Arab armies united by Islam destroyed the Roman field army at the Yarmuk in 636 and took Egypt by 641, removing in six years the provinces that had paid for the army, and what remained was a Greek state of Anatolia and the Aegean.
chapters.s2: Arab forces raided Palestine from 634 and beat a Roman army at Ajnadayn; at the Yarmuk in August 636 they destroyed the field army Heraclius had rebuilt, and he withdrew from Syria. Patriarch Sophronius surrendered Jerusalem to Caliph Umar in person in 637 or 638. Amr ibn al-As entered Egypt in December 639 with about 4,000 men, the fortress of Babylon fell in April 641, two months after Heraclius died, and the last Roman troops left Alexandria in September 642. The conquerors kept the Roman tax registers, written in Greek, and the Greek-speaking clerks who ran them until the turn of the eighth century. The surviving empire began to settle its armies on Anatolian land in the districts later called themes, replacing much of the cash pay that its revenue could no longer cover.

stories.today: The Greek Orthodox Patriarchates of Antioch, seated in Damascus since the fourteenth century, and of Alexandria are the main institutional survivors of Roman rule in the provinces lost between 636 and 642. The Theodosian land walls are part of the Historic Areas of Istanbul, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1985.

arc.title: Conquest Undid the Republic
arc.sub: Rome from the expulsion of the kings to Augustus, 509 to 27 BCE
arc.thesis: The Republic's institutions shared the rewards of war among a competing aristocracy, a citizen militia and Italian allies, and that bargain conquered Italy and then the Mediterranean; once the rewards of conquest came from overseas and at scale, they flowed to individual commanders and their armies, and the institutions that had won the empire could no longer govern the men who ran it.
assumptions: Assumes the sources for the early Republic, written down three to four centuries later, preserve the outline of real institutions even where the stories are invented.
Assumes the fall was structural; a case can be made that it was the contingent outcome of a few men's choices between 60 and 44 BCE, and that the system was functioning in 63.
Assumes the Gracchan account of a dispossessed Italian peasantry is broadly right, which field survey of the Italian countryside has made contestable.
arc.disconfirm: If the thesis were wrong, the Republic should have broken under the strain of losing wars as readily as winning them, or the armies that marched on Rome should have been indifferent to their generals' fortunes. The test cases run the thesis's way: the Republic survived Cannae with its institutions intact, and every army that marched on Rome between 88 and 43 BCE did so for a commander who controlled its pay, its plunder or its discharge.
arc.awkward: The Republic's fastest conquests, from 200 to 146 BCE, coincided with its most stable politics: no army entered Rome and no tribune was killed while Macedon, the Seleucids and Carthage were broken. The thesis needs a lag of two generations between cause and effect and has to explain it.
